## Is my result real? {#is-my-result-real}

<p class="eyebrow">A report from the lab</p>
<p class="opening-report">“We treated cells with compound Q.<br>We measured enzyme activity.<br>n = 6 replicates.”</p>

::: notes
**Time: 13:30–13:32 (2 minutes).**

**Say:** Give only the three statements on screen. Do not supply a cell line, dose, time, control, plot or protocol yet. This is an incomplete fictional lab report, worded the way a methods section or figure legend typically reads. Ask what the audience would need to know before interpreting it. Let someone question “replicates”; do not immediately define it for them. If necessary, ask what exactly was repeated six times.

**Context (not yet revealed):** L1 is a human cell line stably expressing kinase Q. Compound Q is a selective ATP-competitive inhibitor of kinase Q. The assay measures kinase Q activity (substrate phosphorylation rate, U/mg protein). These details are revealed progressively from slide 3 onward.

**Conceptual point:** A familiar methods phrase can conceal very different experimental structures. Missing information must be requested before a claim can be evaluated.

**Likely misconception:** “Replicates” unambiguously means six independent experiments. In practice the word is used for anything from repeated readings or separate wells to separate experiment days. At this stage we cannot tell what it means.

**Optional follow-up:** What claim does this experiment permit, with only this information?

**Sources:** AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 17, 73–74, 121–122. New fictional wording; no results or source data are displayed.
:::

## Six of what? {#six-of-what .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Compare interpretations · 2 minutes</p>
<p class="big">What could “6 replicates” mean?</p>
<div class="triplicate-options fragment">
<p>Six readings of one sample?</p>
<p>Six cultures from one passage, treated on the same day?</p>
<p>Six separately initiated preparations, on different days?</p>
</div>
<p class="fine">Possible meanings, not yet the protocol for this experiment.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 13:32–13:36 (4 minutes).**

**Say:** Give pairs two minutes to propose at least two meanings, without revealing the examples. Advance once to display the possibilities. Use two minutes to hear what information would distinguish them. All are plausible uses of the word. Do not yet say which one applies, introduce technical vocabulary or ask for a numerical N. The next slide provides the first notebook detail.

**Conceptual point:** The word “replicates” does not identify what was repeated. Six readings of one sample share everything; six preparations on different days share much less. Different meanings support different claims.

**Likely misconception:** The best-sounding interpretation is probably the intended one. We must check the experimental record instead.

**Optional follow-up:** What single question would you ask the person who did the experiment?

**Sources:** A pp. 73–74, 121–122; R p. 13. Adapted ambiguity exercise, not a copied source slide.
:::

## The tube is the experimental unit {#assignment-unit}

<div class="two-col">
<div><div class="tubes"><div class="tube v">V</div><div class="tube q">Q</div></div><p class="small" style="text-align:center;margin-top:24px">Two tubes from preparation P1</p></div>
<div><p class="big">The culture tube</p><p class="medium">Our experimental unit</p><p class="small">We assign one tube to each condition within a preparation.</p></div>
</div>
<p class="takeaway keyline">The preparation connects the tubes as a pair.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 13:39–13:41 (2 minutes).**

**Say:** The treatment enters at the tube level. That makes the tube the experimental or treatment-assignment unit here. Allocation is constrained within each preparation: one tube gets vehicle and one compound. The preparation is a block, so the two tube outcomes share a history. Later we compare them within that pair.

**Conceptual point:** Assignment unit and unit used for a biological comparison need not be identical. An experimental unit does not imply that all outcomes are uncorrelated.

**Likely misconception:** Calling the tube an experimental unit means its outcome is unrelated to the other tube’s outcome. Pairing must be preserved.

**Optional follow-up:** If treatment were assigned to an entire plate, what would change?

**Sources:** A pp. 121–122, 137–144; R pp. 59–62. Terminology made explicit for this defined design.
:::

<div><div class="count">6</div><div class="count-label">paired biological comparisons</div></div>
</div>

::: notes
**Time: 13:41–13:48 (7 minutes).**

**Say:** Reveal that the same split was repeated with six cultures initiated and maintained separately, all from L1. Allow two minutes to draw the hierarchy and decide on counts. Spend three minutes hearing explanations before revealing the 36/12/6 answer. Use two further minutes to ask what each number counts. Each preparation contributes a vehicle-versus-Q comparison. Do not announce that the six comparisons must be independent; we have not yet inspected what they share across days. Ask for a report with nouns, not a bare N.

**Conceptual point:** The number depends on the unit. Twelve assigned tubes form six paired biological comparisons, with 36 assay readings.

**Likely misconception:** The largest count is the biological sample size, or separate preparation labels alone establish independence. The replication and shared-variation discussion follows.

**Optional follow-up:** What claim does this experiment permit if the 36 measurements come from only these six preparations?

## Technical and biological replication are different {#replication}

<div class="replication">
<div><p class="medium">The assay on one lysate</p><div class="reading-row" style="justify-content:flex-start"><i class="dot"></i><i class="dot"></i><i class="dot"></i></div><p>Technical replication</p><p class="small">How much does the measurement vary?</p></div>
<div><p class="medium">The culture preparation</p><div class="repeat-preps"><div class="prep">P1</div><div class="prep">P2</div><div class="prep">P3</div></div><p>Biological replication</p><p class="small">How much does the result vary across preparations?</p></div>
</div>

<p class="takeaway keyline">What claim does this experiment permit?</p>

::: notes
**Time: 13:48–13:52 (4 minutes).**

**Say:** Use two minutes for the audience to explain what each repetition tells us and two minutes to debrief. Repeating the assay helps us examine the measurement process. Independently initiated preparations let us see variation in the biological system as defined here. Neither is useless; they answer different questions. All preparations remain from cell line L1. Return to the question on screen: six preparations can speak to repetition within this system, while three assay aliquots alone cannot establish repetition across preparations.

**Conceptual point:** What is repeated determines which sources of variation are represented.

**Likely misconception:** Technical replication is bad practice, or biological replication automatically samples different people. Both claims are wrong. The distinction is contextual and depends on the target claim.

**Optional follow-up:** Which repeat would address concern about an inconsistent plate reader? Which would address inconsistent culture responses?

**Sources:** A pp. 12, 68, 73–74, 121–122; R p. 53. No outlier removal or inference is taught here.
:::

## How many data points do we really have? {#data-points-concept}

<p class="medium">36 readings. 12 tubes. 6 preparations.</p>
<p class="medium fragment">Treat all 36 as separate biological evidence<br>and your analysis looks far more certain than it is.</p>
<p class="takeaway fragment">The number of measurements and the amount of evidence are not the same thing.</p>
<p class="small fragment">Three aliquots from one lysate all share the same extraction, treatment, and cell history. If the lysate was over-diluted, all three shift together — they do not provide three separate votes on the biology.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 13:52–13:54 (2 minutes).**

**Say:** We just established the 36/12/6 hierarchy. Now ask: if someone analysed all 36 readings as 36 separate biological observations, what would happen? The analysis would appear very precise — narrow uncertainty, confident conclusions — but that precision would be false, because most of it reflects measurement variation within a single lysate, not biological variation across preparations. This is not a rare mistake; it has a name — pseudoreplication — and it appears routinely in the literature. The point to land before the exercise: counting measurements is not the same as counting independent biological events. Two readings can look completely separate — different well positions, different labels, different numbers — and still carry the same biological information if they came from the same source. The exercise on the next slide asks exactly that question.

**Conceptual point:** Inflating N by treating shared-source observations as independent produces overconfident statistical conclusions — intervals that are too narrow, p-values that are too small.

**Likely misconception:** More measurements always mean more evidence. They do — about the thing that was repeated. Technical replicates give more evidence about the measurement; biological replicates about the biology.

**Optional follow-up:** Name one published paper in your field where the reported N seemed surprisingly large for the described biology.

**Sources:** Lazic (2010) *J Neurosci Methods* 187:180–183 — pseudoreplication in neuroscience; Lazic et al. (2018) *BMC Neurosci* 19:9; A pp. 17, 119; R pp. 8, 33.
:::

## Which observations are independent? {#independence .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Which pairs share a source of variation?</p>
<div class="comparison-row"><span class="letter">A</span><span>Two readings</span><span>from one lysate</span></div>
<div class="comparison-row"><span class="letter">B</span><span>Vehicle and compound</span><span>from one preparation</span></div>
<div class="comparison-row"><span class="letter">C</span><span>Two preparations</span><span>measured on the same day</span></div>

::: notes
**Time: 13:54–13:57 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Use one minute of pair discussion and two minutes of debrief. A shares a lysate; B shares its preparation and possibly day; C can share day conditions. Do not simply label C independent. Independence is about the process and model, not the distance between dots or their different identifiers. For C, introduce only that some preparations were measured on the same day. The next slide reveals the full day layout. No numerical plot is needed: the shared sources follow from the experimental history.

**Conceptual point:** Shared sources of variation can make outcomes dependent. Independent technical measurement errors do not turn shared biological material into independent treatment evidence.

**Likely misconception:** Different wells or different labels ensure independence, or a statistical test can certify independence from a small dataset.

**Optional follow-up:** What change to the day's reagents might move several values together?

**Sources:** A pp. 17, 119, 121–122; R pp. 8, 33, 53. The exercise completes the hierarchy discussion without a formal dependence model.
:::

<div class="day"><p class="day-name">Day 2</p><div class="pair-row"><span>P3</span><span class="pair-mark"><i class="dot"></i><i class="tri"></i></span></div><div class="pair-row"><span>P4</span><span class="pair-mark"><i class="dot"></i><i class="tri"></i></span></div></div>
<div class="day"><p class="day-name">Day 3</p><div class="pair-row"><span>P5</span><span class="pair-mark"><i class="dot"></i><i class="tri"></i></span></div><div class="pair-row"><span>P6</span><span class="pair-mark"><i class="dot"></i><i class="tri"></i></span></div></div>
</div>

<p class="takeaway fragment">A shift affecting both conditions equally cancels in their difference.</p>

<!-- REVIEW: Six independent pair contrasts are a teaching-model assumption, not an empirical finding. A day-specific treatment response would induce dependence between the two contrasts on that day. Retain this qualification when editing. -->
::: notes
**Time: 13:57–14:00 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** This is the final notebook reveal: two preparation pairs on each day, with both conditions in every pair. Ask the audience to trace one within-day comparison. A change in conditions between days is a batch effect. If a day adds the same amount to both conditions, subtraction removes that component. Ask what happens if Q's response itself differs by day.

**Conceptual point:** The layout separates treatment from day. Pairing can remove a shared additive shift, but does not eliminate all possible batch effects.

**Likely misconception:** Six contrasts are universally independent, or blocking removes every batch problem. The simulation assumes independent preparation effects and technical errors, fixed shared additive day shifts, and no day-by-treatment interaction. A shared treatment response by day could correlate the two contrasts on that day. Independence would then need a different model or more independent days.

**Optional follow-up:** If the compound degrades on one day, will the difference still be unaffected?

**Sources:** A pp. 190–192; R pp. 8, 62. The universal “ideal design” claims in the sources are deliberately not reused. Keep the arithmetic illustration to words; the model details remain in notes.
:::

## What if controls ran on Monday? {#confounding}

<p class="eyebrow">A different, hypothetical layout</p>
<div class="day-grid fault" role="img" aria-label="Hypothetical confounded design: all vehicle tubes on Monday, all compound tubes on Tuesday, with no within-day treatment comparison.">
<div class="day"><p class="day-name">Monday</p><div class="pair-mark"><i class="dot"></i><i class="dot"></i><i class="dot"></i><i class="dot"></i><i class="dot"></i><i class="dot"></i></div><p>All vehicle tubes</p></div>
<div class="day"><p class="day-name">Tuesday</p><div class="pair-mark"><i class="tri"></i><i class="tri"></i><i class="tri"></i><i class="tri"></i><i class="tri"></i><i class="tri"></i></div><p>All compound tubes</p></div>
</div>
<p class="takeaway fragment">Treatment and day change together. Which caused the difference?</p>

::: notes
**Time: 14:00–14:03 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Explicitly announce that this is not our actual protocol. It is a hypothetical scheduling shortcut. Give pairs time to identify the missing comparison. Without within-day treatment comparisons, a difference could arise from treatment, day, or both. Label this confounding only after the audience explains the problem. Give the layout comparison its full three minutes. Close the first 35-minute section with “What claim does this experiment permit?” A treatment-specific claim cannot be separated from a day effect in this alternative layout.

**Conceptual point:** Complete treatment/day confounding prevents separating their effects from these observations alone. More readings of the same lysates do not create the missing comparison.

**Likely misconception:** A later calculation can recover both effects without new information or strong external assumptions. Also avoid suggesting that every batch effect is complete confounding.

**Optional follow-up:** What is the smallest change to the schedule that creates a treatment comparison within a day?

**Sources:** R pp. 6–8, 59–62; A pp. 187–192. New schematic. No questionable numerical claims imported.
:::

## What does “the compound works” mean? {#claim}

<p class="quote">“Compound Q works.”</p>
<p class="medium">What claim does this experiment permit?</p>
<p class="takeaway fragment keyline">Enzyme activity in L1 lysates after 24 hours.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 14:03–14:06 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** We can now describe the experiment, but what was it intended to establish? Read the lab-meeting claim aloud. Invite two interpretations of “works.” Then reveal the endpoint. This assay addresses activity in a particular preparation under particular conditions; it does not by itself demonstrate a mechanism or clinical benefit.

**Conceptual point:** A measured endpoint is connected to a biological hypothesis but is not synonymous with it.

**Likely misconception:** A well-controlled difference automatically validates the strongest interpretation of the experiment.

**Optional follow-up:** Could enzyme activity change for a reason other than direct inhibition of the enzyme?

**Sources:** A p. 189; R pp. 4, 6–7; D pp. 19–21, 52. Compound and cell line are fictional; possible mechanisms are questions, not assertions.
:::

## What quantity are we trying to learn? {#target-quantity}

<p class="small">For each preparation, after 24 hours</p>
<div class="effect-line"><span class="compound">Activity with Q</span><b>−</b><span class="vehicle">Activity with vehicle</span></div>
<p class="big">The average difference<br>across preparations of L1</p>
<p class="small keyline">Units: U/mg protein. Negative means lower activity with Q.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 14:06–14:09 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** We need to state the quantity we want to learn about. Within each preparation, compare the activity with Q against its vehicle tube. Then our target is the mean of that difference across the relevant population of preparations under these conditions. Keep the language as “the quantity we want to learn.” Do not introduce a technical name or teach how to compute an average. The target is the average biological change across relevant preparations, not the number of measurements. We are defining the question, not summarizing data.

**Conceptual point:** State contrast direction, endpoint, time and biological unit before inference. Distinguish the observed sample estimate from the population target.

**Likely misconception:** “Effect” necessarily means a clinical benefit or a specific mechanism. Our chosen effect here is an absolute mean difference on the assay scale.

**Optional follow-up:** Would the same quantity answer a question about activity after a different incubation time?

**Sources:** A pp. 136–141, 189; D p. 52. Mean-difference concept only; effect estimation and uncertainty remain in the later approved section.
:::

## Which future experiments should this inform? {#sample-population}

<div class="scope">
<div><p class="small">Our sample</p><div class="sample-preps"><div class="prep">P1</div><div class="prep">P2</div><div class="prep">P3</div><div class="prep">P4</div><div class="prep">P5</div><div class="prep">P6</div></div></div>
<div class="population"><p class="medium">Further preparations<br>of cell line L1</p><p class="small">Under the culture and assay<br>conditions we have specified</p></div>
</div>
<p class="takeaway keyline">The population can be a set of possible experimental preparations.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 14:09–14:13 (4 minutes).**

**Say:** Six preparations are the ones we observed. Our question usually reaches beyond them to preparations we might make next. That collection of possible preparations, under defined culture and assay conditions, is a target population. It need not be a population of people. Ask which conditions should be held fixed and which may vary within the claim.

**Conceptual point:** In laboratory biology, a population is defined by the scope of the intended inference and the process that could generate new experimental units.

**Likely misconception:** Repeating a single cell line samples the population of all human cells, or the population is automatically everything in the incubator.

**Optional follow-up:** Would a new serum lot still fall inside your intended claim?

**Sources:** R pp. 16–33, especially 30–33; A pp. 56–58, 63, 71; D pp. 9–20. Rebuilt sampling-space idea with the recurring assay rather than M&Ms or BMI data.
:::

## What population would you claim this applies to? {#population-question .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Choose a claim and defend its limits · 3 minutes</p>
<div class="claim-options">
<div class="claim-option"><b>A</b><span>Further L1 preparations under these conditions</span></div>
<div class="claim-option"><b>B</b><span>Other cell lines and donors</span></div>
<div class="claim-option"><b>C</b><span>Patients receiving the compound</span></div>
</div>
<p class="takeaway fragment">What would you need to know before choosing A?</p>

::: notes
**Time: 14:13–14:21 (8 minutes).**

**Say:** Three minutes in pairs, three minutes hearing two arguments, two minutes to debrief. A is the intended narrow target, not a guaranteed extrapolation. Ask whether the six preparations and three days cover the conditions they mean by “these conditions,” and whether selection, QC or unrecorded batches matter. Fold the previous separate scope-of-replication slide into this debrief: repeated preparations of L1 cover preparation variation; other cell lines or donors require additional biological sampling, and a claim across laboratories needs evidence relevant to laboratories. More assay readings of these lysates cannot supply those missing systems. B requires sampling additional biological systems. C requires a much broader chain of evidence; do not turn this into a clinical-trial lecture.

**Conceptual point:** A claim's population must match what was sampled and the assumptions used to extend beyond it. More distant generalizations require additional evidence.

**Likely misconception:** A is automatically justified once N is reported, or any in-vitro result directly represents patients.

**Optional follow-up:** What difference between your sampled preparations and future preparations worries you most?

**Sources:** R pp. 27–33, 45–47; A pp. 63, 71; D pp. 18–20. This is the approved eight-minute claim/population exercise. Do not introduce numerical inference to decide representativity.
:::

## Which observations describe the treatment response? {#response-unit .interaction}


<p class="prompt-tag">Carry the design into the data · 2 minutes in pairs</p>
<p class="medium">“We now understand the experiment.<br>Before testing anything, what actually happened?”</p>
<div class="allocation">
<div><p>One value per tube</p><p class="small">The three assay aliquots have already been summarized.</p></div>
<div><p>One change per preparation</p><p class="small">Compound Q minus its paired vehicle.</p></div>
</div>
<p class="takeaway fragment">Six preparations contribute six paired changes.</p>


::: notes
**Time: 14:21–14:26 (5 minutes).**

**Say:** The opening block is complete. Use these five minutes to connect its design to the observations we will describe. Give pairs two minutes to identify the relevant change and three minutes to debrief. Each tube contributes the arithmetic average of its three technical readings; no aliquots were omitted. Each preparation then supplies one Q-minus-vehicle comparison. This preprocessing respects the simple balanced assay design. The term average is familiar language here; its definition comes later. Ask which experimental space the six preparations cover. The data follow on the next slide.

**Conceptual point:** The six biological responses are paired changes. Twelve tube summaries are their ingredients; 36 technical readings are not 36 treatment responses.

**Likely misconception:** Summarizing assay repeats loses six biological experiments or establishes independence. The original raw readings remain available, and the dependence caveat from the earlier block still applies.

**Optional follow-up:** Which count belongs beside a summary of the treatment response?

**Sources:** AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 73–74, 121–122, adapted to the current protocol. Bridge from design to data.

:::

## How large is each preparation’s change? {#six-changes .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Observe · describe to a neighbour · 1 minute</p>
<img class="data-plot" src="figures/generated/bio-changes.png" alt="The six Q-minus-vehicle changes: P1 about minus 20.9, P2 about zero, P3 minus 17.7, P4 minus 23.7, P5 plus 6.0, P6 minus 6.2 U/mg protein." />
<p class="takeaway">Are the changes similar? Is one unusual? Does one point drive the picture?</p><p class="fine">Simulated L1 assay. Six independently initiated preparations, each contributing one paired comparison.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 14:29–14:32 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Use one minute of paired observation and two minutes for a debrief. The horizontal reference marks equal observed activities in a pair. Negative values mean lower activity with Q. Four reductions range from about 6 to 24 U/mg, one comparison is nearly unchanged, and P5 goes upwards. P4 has the largest reduction. The downward direction appears in several preparations, not just P4. P5 is worth asking about; an opposite direction is not itself proof of a mistake. No deletion or formal leave-one-out procedure is needed.

**Conceptual point:** One observed change per preparation answers the response question while preserving heterogeneity.

**Likely misconception:** All six changes should be alike if an average response exists, or an opposite-direction result should be discarded.

**Optional follow-up:** Which preparation would you inspect in the notebook first, and why?

**Sources:** AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 25, 41, 73–74. All six changes are retained.

:::

## The average and the middle answer different questions {#mean-and-median}

<img class="data-plot short-plot" src="figures/generated/changes-centres.png" alt="Six ordered paired changes with mean at minus 10.4 and median at minus 11.9 U/mg protein." />
<div class="definitions-pair">
<div><p class="compound">Mean: -10.4 U/mg</p><p class="small">Add all six changes, then divide by six.</p></div>
<div><p class="vehicle">Median: -11.9 U/mg</p><p class="small">Order the changes; average the two middle values.</p></div>
</div><p class="fine">Simulated L1 assay. Six independently initiated preparations, each contributing one paired comparison.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 14:32–14:35 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** The mean is -10.4 U/mg and uses every observed magnitude. The median is -11.9 U/mg: with six observations, it is halfway between the third and fourth ordered changes, about −17.68 and −6.18. Use the dots to illustrate the average as a balance point and the median as the middle position. The mean is a natural description of an average quantitative change, especially with approximately symmetric values; the median describes the middle. Our original scientific question concerned an average difference, so retain that distinction rather than swapping targets for a nicer number.

**Conceptual point:** Mean and median are complementary descriptions with different responses to extreme magnitudes.

**Likely misconception:** An asymmetric pattern always requires the median, or the median estimates the same quantity as the mean in every setting.

**Optional follow-up:** Which summary uses how far P5 lies from the other changes?

**Sources:** AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 33–35. The categorical skewed-means-median rule is deliberately not reused.

:::

## What is a quartile? {#quantiles-intro}

<p class="medium">Sort the values. Cut them into four groups of equal size.</p>
<img class="data-plot" src="figures/generated/quartiles-boxplot.png" alt="Twelve sorted values in four groups of three. Dashed cuts between the groups are labelled Q1, Q2 = median and Q3. Below, a box plot built from the same cuts: the box runs from Q1 to Q3 with a line at the median and holds the middle half of the values; lines reach out to the lowest and highest quarter." />
<p class="takeaway fragment">The three cuts are the quartiles. A box plot draws them: the box holds the middle half of the values.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 14:35–14:37 (2 minutes).**

**Say:** Start with the dots: twelve values, sorted from smallest to largest. Cut them into four groups with the same number of values — three each, so each group holds a quarter. The three cuts are the quartiles. The first cut, Q1, has a quarter of the values below it. The middle cut, Q2, has half below it — that is the median we just met. The third cut, Q3, has three quarters below it. Then move to the bottom half of the figure: a box plot is simply a drawing of these cuts. The box runs from Q1 to Q3, so it always contains the middle half of the values; the line inside is the median; the lines on either side reach out to the lowest and highest quarter. Do not explain how software places the cut when the values do not divide evenly — conventions differ slightly and it does not matter here.

**Conceptual point:** Quartiles are the cut points that split sorted data into four equal-sized groups; a box plot is a picture of them.

**Likely misconception:** The box contains most of the data, or quartiles need a formula. The box always holds the middle half — no more, no less.

**Optional follow-up:** If we added one very large value, which part of the box plot would move most?

**Sources:** AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 36–40. Figure: scripts/generate_quartiles.R (illustrative values).
:::

## How far do changes lie from their mean? {#variance-and-sd}


<div class="data-split">
<div><img class="data-plot" src="figures/generated/changes-deviations.png" alt="Six paired changes and their distances from the mean. A vertical mean line is orange; horizontal distances are teal." /></div>
<div><p>Variance</p><p class="small">Summarizes squared distances from the mean.</p>
<p class="keyline">Standard deviation</p><p class="small">The square root puts spread back in the measurement units.</p>
<p class="medium fragment">SD = 12.1 U/mg</p></div></div><p class="fine">Simulated L1 assay. Six independently initiated preparations, each contributing one paired comparison.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 14:37–14:40 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Point to the mean line and the distance to each preparation’s change. Squaring distances makes them nonnegative and gives large deviations greater influence. Sample variance sums these squared deviations and divides by n−1, here five; its value is 147.5 in squared activity units. SD is its square root, 12.1 U/mg. Mention the sample denominator once in speech if needed, with no derivation or exercise. We are describing spread among the six changes, not the precision of their mean. Avoid a percentage-within-one-SD rule for these six values.

**Conceptual point:** Variance quantifies squared deviations; SD expresses that spread in the same units as the changes.

**Likely misconception:** SD is the ordinary mean absolute distance, or an interval describing how well the average is known.

**Optional follow-up:** Which preparation contributes a large squared deviation from this mean?

**Sources:** AppliedStats_2026.pdf p. 40. Uses sample variance with n−1; official R sd documentation confirms the convention.

:::

## Which plot preserves the information we need? {#paired-or-box}


<div class="plot-compare">
<div><p>The paired values</p><img class="data-plot" src="figures/generated/bio-pairs-compact.png" alt="Twelve tube summaries connected as six pairs, retaining baseline activity and direction." /><p class="small">Starting values and within-preparation change.</p></div>
<div><p>The six changes</p><img class="data-plot" src="figures/generated/changes-boxpoints.png" alt="A horizontal boxplot of the six paired changes with all six raw change points overlaid." /><p class="small">A compact summary, with every change visible.</p></div>
</div>
<p class="fine">Same original simulated assay. Left: 12 tube values forming six pairs. Right: six Q-minus-vehicle changes.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 14:40–14:43 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** The paired plot preserves both activities and the relationship within a preparation. The boxplot summarizes the six differences rather than treating the two conditions as unpaired groups. Explain that the box runs from Q1 to Q3, and its central line is the median. Whiskers extend to observed values within 1.5 IQR of the quartiles; here they reach the observed extremes. All six points are shown, including those overlaid near the median or whiskers. With six changes, the raw observations carry essential information. A boxplot alone would hide it. Do not read its whiskers as a precision interval or treat points outside whiskers as automatic errors.

**Conceptual point:** The plot should preserve the experimental relationship and the individual observations relevant to the question.

**Likely misconception:** A boxplot includes every important feature, or pairing is unnecessary once values are summarized.

**Optional follow-up:** Which view lets you see that a large change started from a high activity level?

**Sources:** AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 25, 38–39, 123, 139. Boxplot of paired changes with raw points, not a copied source layout.

:::

## How would you describe this result to a colleague? {#describe-result .interaction}


<p class="prompt-tag">Write two sentences · 1 minute</p>
<p class="medium">Direction and size.<br>Variation and any unusual preparation.<br>What the six observations count.</p>
<div class="fragment keyline">
<p class="small">Four preparations decreased, one was almost unchanged and one increased.<br>The mean paired change was -10.4 U/mg, with SD 12.1 U/mg across six independently initiated L1 preparations.</p></div>
<p class="fine">Describes these simulated observations; does not establish a mechanism or generalize beyond the stated experimental space.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 14:43–14:46 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Give one minute to write and one minute to hear a response. Reveal one acceptable description for the final minute. Four preparations decrease, P2 is nearly unchanged, P5 increases; the largest decrease is P4. The mean is -10.4 and SD 12.1 U/mg. Participants may additionally use median -11.9, IQR 18.6, or the observed span if they say what those summaries describe. They should not imply that every preparation decreased or that Q has a proven mechanism. Ask whether the wording faithfully preserves heterogeneity.

**Conceptual point:** A useful descriptive report combines magnitude, variability, exceptions and an explicit replication count.

**Likely misconception:** A summary sentence must choose either raw observations or numerical summaries, rather than use both.

**Optional follow-up:** What claim does this experiment permit from this description alone?

**Sources:** AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 50, 81, rebuilt as a short reporting task.

:::

## Six preparations give one estimate {#one-sample-estimate}

<img class="data-plot short-plot" src="figures/generated/unc-observed.png" alt="Six original paired changes and their mean, minus 10.4 U/mg." />
<p class="takeaway">Our estimate from this particular experiment: <strong>−10.4 U/mg</strong></p>
<p class="fine">Simulated L1 assay · Q minus vehicle · six independently initiated preparations.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 14:46–14:48 (2 minutes).**

**Say:** Return to the six unchanged paired changes. Each is a Q-minus-vehicle contrast after technical repeats were averaged within each tube. The vertical line is their mean, −10.4 U/mg. Our target is the average paired effect across the specified L1 preparation process. The sample gives an estimate of that quantity, not its known population value. Preserve the culture conditions, dose and 24-hour endpoint from the opening.

**Conceptual point:** A particular sample gives a particular estimate of the population quantity.

**Likely misconception:** The average of these six is automatically the exact average over all relevant preparations.

**Optional follow-up:** Which number here belongs to one preparation, and which summarizes the experiment?

**Sources:** AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 56–62, 67, 75–80; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 37–44; DoctaMed.pdf pp. 10–17. Concepts rebuilt using the recurring assay; probability wording corrected according to CONTENT_MAP.md. 

:::

## New preparations, new mean {#new-preparations-new-mean}

<img class="data-plot" src="figures/generated/unc-three-repeats.png" alt="Three simulated repetitions with six preparation changes each; diamonds show each repetition’s different mean." />
<p class="takeaway">Six dots → one mean in each repetition</p>
<p class="small">In a simulation we choose the truth: here the true mean effect is set to <strong>−14 U/mg</strong>. Our real estimate (−10.4) is one draw from experiments like these.</p>
<p class="fine">Dark dots: preparations. Rust diamonds: experiment means.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 14:48–14:51 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Trace one row: six paired changes become one diamond. Then compare three rows. These are the first three repetitions from the fixed seed, not selected examples. In our teaching simulation we know the true average: −14 U/mg. The experiment’s estimate need not equal it. This value was already in the original data-generating model; it was not fitted to −10.4. The generator preserves normal preparation effects (SD 9), tube errors (SD 3), three technical errors (SD 2.5) and two-decimal assay rounding. Shared additive preparation and day baselines cancel in paired differences, apart from negligible rounding. There is no treatment-by-day variation. Real experiments do not give us a known truth.

**Conceptual point:** Different sample means can come from the same fixed underlying population mean.

**Likely misconception:** The moving diamonds mean the true effect changes between experiments.

**Optional follow-up:** If you saw only one row, would you know exactly where the fixed true mean lies?

**Sources:** AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 56–62, 67, 75–80; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 37–44; DoctaMed.pdf pp. 10–17. Concepts rebuilt using the recurring assay; probability wording corrected according to CONTENT_MAP.md. 

:::

## What happens when we collect the means? {#sampling-distribution}

<div class="uncertainty-stack">
<img data-fragment-index="0" class="data-plot fragment fade-out" src="figures/generated/unc-means-10.png" alt="Means from the first ten repeated experiments." /><img data-fragment-index="0" class="data-plot fragment fade-in-then-out" src="figures/generated/unc-means-100.png" alt="Means accumulated from the first one hundred experiments." /><img data-fragment-index="1" class="data-plot fragment" src="figures/generated/unc-means-10000.png" alt="Means from ten thousand experiments, each containing six preparation changes." />
</div>
<p class="takeaway">A <strong>sampling distribution</strong>: estimates across repeated experiments</p>
<p class="fine">Every entry is one experiment’s mean, not one preparation. Same horizontal scale at every reveal.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 14:51–14:54 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Reveal 10, then 100, then 10,000 accumulated means. Each comes from six newly generated paired changes. The frequency scale is a fraction of experiments so panels remain comparable as repetitions accumulate. Point to the fixed −14 line. Name this the sampling distribution of the mean. This is not the shape of our original six measurements, and it is not a probability distribution for possible true means. Simulation approximates what repeated sampling under the known model would generate; it does not turn our one observed experiment into 10,000 real replications.

**Conceptual point:** The distribution of an estimator across hypothetical repetitions is distinct from the distribution of observations.

**Likely misconception:** The histogram contains 10,000 additional biological observations from our actual study, or the true mean itself varies.

**Optional follow-up:** What has to be done in the lab to generate one new entry in this histogram?

**Sources:** AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 56–62, 67, 75–80; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 37–44; DoctaMed.pdf pp. 10–17. Concepts rebuilt using the recurring assay; probability wording corrected according to CONTENT_MAP.md. 

:::

## Preparations vary more than their mean does {#sd-versus-se}

<img class="data-plot" src="figures/generated/unc-sd-se.png" alt="Left: spread of simulated preparation responses. Right: narrower spread of simulated six-preparation means, on identical horizontal axes." />
<div class="definitions-pair"><p class="small"><strong>SD</strong> · spread of preparation responses</p><p class="small"><strong>SE</strong> · spread of the estimated mean across repetitions</p></div>
<p class="fine">Both panels use the same simulation model. Each experiment on the right has n = 6.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 14:54–14:57 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Spend one minute asking what one contribution represents on each side. The left pools preparation responses from the repeated simulations; the right contains one mean per experiment. Both horizontal axes are identical. The spread of the means is the standard error of this estimator. Simulated response SD is about 10.2 U/mg; simulated SD of means is about 4.1 U/mg. These are model repetition results, not the original sample’s SD of 12.1 or its estimated SE. Variation among individual responses and variability of their estimated average answer different questions. This is not a recommendation to replace raw observations with SEM error bars.

**Conceptual point:** SE is the standard deviation of an estimator’s sampling distribution; SD describes the observations.

**Likely misconception:** SE is an improved replacement for SD, or smaller SE means individual preparations respond more consistently.

**Optional follow-up:** Which spread would help describe how differently two preparations might respond?

**Sources:** AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 56–62, 67, 75–80; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 37–44; DoctaMed.pdf pp. 10–17. Concepts rebuilt using the recurring assay; probability wording corrected according to CONTENT_MAP.md. 

:::

## How can one experiment estimate that spread? {#estimate-the-se}

<p class="medium">For independent preparation-level changes:</p>
<p class="uncertainty-equation">SE(mean) = SD / √n</p>
<p class="takeaway fragment">Our estimated SE: 12.1 / √6 ≈ <strong>4.96 U/mg</strong></p>
<p class="fine">SD is the sample SD of paired changes. n counts preparation pairs, not technical readings.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 14:57–14:59 (2 minutes).**

**Say:** Only now show the formula. The true SE uses the population SD; we estimate it by substituting the sample SD. Using full precision, 12.1445/sqrt(6)=4.9580 U/mg. Display rounding gives 5.0. This estimate need not equal the simulated long-run SE of about 4.1: the six observed responses are themselves a variable sample. The formula requires independent, identically distributed contrasts with finite variance. It is not automatically valid for shared treatment-by-day responses, clustered preparations, or correlated repeated measures. Normality is not needed for this variance identity; the small-sample t interval introduced next uses a stronger distributional assumption.

**Conceptual point:** A sample can estimate sampling variability, under the experimental and statistical structure assumed.

**Likely misconception:** The denominator can use 36 assay readings, or the same formula applies unchanged to any dependent observations.

**Optional follow-up:** What part of our earlier discussion of days makes this calculation conditional?

**Sources:** AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 56–62, 67, 75–80; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 37–44; DoctaMed.pdf pp. 10–17. Concepts rebuilt using the recurring assay; probability wording corrected according to CONTENT_MAP.md. 

:::

## Can we show a range around our estimate? {#from-se-to-interval}

<p class="small">Instead of giving only our best estimate, can we show a range of values compatible with its uncertainty?</p>
<div class="fragment"><img class="data-plot short-plot" src="figures/generated/unc-observed-ci.png" alt="Observed mean minus 10.4 with a 95 percent t-based confidence interval from minus 23.2 to plus 2.3 U/mg." /></div>
<p class="takeaway">A 95% confidence interval for the <strong>mean paired effect</strong></p>
<p class="fine">Assumes independent, approximately normal paired changes under this L1 protocol.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 14:59–15:01 (2 minutes).**

**Say:** Motivate the range before revealing it. An interval combines the best estimate and uncertainty in that estimate. This is a paired t interval, calculated on the six differences, not separate intervals around vehicle and compound. The offline calculation is mean ± qt(0.975,5) × sample SD/sqrt(6), with multiplier 2.5706 and margin 12.7449 U/mg. At n=6 a generic two-SE shortcut is too narrow. Explain the method’s name briefly without a derivation. Exact nominal coverage requires independent normal differences; the existing Gaussian generator meets this before negligible measurement rounding. Six observations cannot establish approximate normality. Real data would require substantive checks of the model and dependence.

**Conceptual point:** An interval estimates the population mean effect, not the spread of individual preparation responses.

**Likely misconception:** The interval should contain 95% of preparation responses, or mean ± one SE is a 95% interval.

**Optional follow-up:** Whose uncertainty does this line represent: one preparation’s response or the average response?

**Sources:** AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 56–62, 67, 75–80; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 37–44; DoctaMed.pdf pp. 10–17. Concepts rebuilt using the recurring assay; probability wording corrected according to CONTENT_MAP.md. NIST/SEMATECH, Confidence Limits for the Mean: https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/eda/section3/eda352.htm (t-based interval and repeated-sampling interpretation).

:::

## What does our interval tell us? {#meaning-of-confidence}

<p class=”big”>Our result: −23 to +2 U/mg.</p>
<p class=”big”>These are the effect sizes the data cannot rule out.</p>
<p class=”takeaway fragment”>The interval shows compatible values — not a probability that the true effect is inside it.</p>
<p class=”small fragment”>Wider interval = less precise estimate, not a worse experiment.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 15:01–15:04 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Point to the numbers first. Minus twenty-three to plus two. Those are the effect sizes we cannot dismiss with this data. Ask participants: does that include zero? Yes. Does it include a ten-unit reduction? Yes. Does it include a twenty-unit reduction? Yes. Everything in that range is compatible with what we observed. The 95% does not mean there is a 95% chance the true effect is somewhere in that interval — the true effect is a fixed number, not a random variable. What varies is the interval itself: if we ran the experiment again, we would get a different interval. Roughly 95% of all such intervals, across many repetitions, would catch the true value. But we do not have many repetitions — we have one, and it either caught it or it did not. The practical message: report the interval, and read it as a range of plausible values.

**Conceptual point:** The interval is a statement about compatible data, not a probability distribution over the true effect.

**Likely misconception:** 95% CI means a 95% chance the true effect is inside this particular interval, or that values outside the interval are impossible.

**Optional follow-up:** If our interval had been −23 to −2 instead, what would change about what we can say?

**Sources:** AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 56–62, 67, 75–80; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 37–44; DoctaMed.pdf pp. 10–17.

:::

## Report the estimate and its precision {#report-se-not-sd .key-message}

<p class="key-label">Key message</p>

<div class="research-paths">
<div><h3>SD — spread of preparations</h3><p>How much do individual<br>preparations vary?</p><p class="small">Describes biological variability<br>across observations.</p></div>
<div><h3>SE or CI — estimate precision</h3><p>How well does the mean<br>characterise the true average?</p><p class="small">Describes how precisely<br>we know the average effect.</p></div>
</div>
<p class="key-statement compact keyline">Reporting an effect? Give the SEM or, better, the 95% CI — not the SD.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 15:04–15:06 (2 minutes).**

**Say:** Many papers still report mean ± SD when describing a treatment effect. The SD is a correct description of preparation-to-preparation variability, but it does not address how confidently the mean has been estimated. If the question is "how large is the effect, and how well do we know it?", the SE or CI is the relevant quantity. A wider CI from six preparations tells the reader more about the reliability of the estimate than an SD does. SD remains appropriate when the goal is genuinely to characterise variability — for instance, describing how heterogeneous a cell population is. The choice depends on the claim.

**Conceptual point:** SD describes scatter in the observations; SE and CI describe precision of the estimate. Match the reported quantity to the question being answered.

**Likely misconception:** SD is always more honest because it is larger, or SE is a corrected version of SD. They describe different things.

**Optional follow-up:** If a collaborator sends you a figure with mean ± SD error bars on a treatment comparison, what would you ask them?

**Sources:** Cumming et al. (2007) J Cell Biol — error bar guidelines. Vaux (2012) Nature. AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 56–62.
:::

## Could this result arise if there were no effect? {#could-this-arise .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Predict before the reveal</p>
<p class="medium">We observed a mean paired change of <strong>−10.4 U/mg</strong>.</p>
<p class="takeaway">What would we expect if the true average treatment effect were exactly zero?</p>
<div class="fragment keyline"><p class="medium">Same variability. Six new preparations.<br>Same paired experiment. True mean <strong>0</strong>.</p></div>
<p class="fine">Hypothetical L1 model: no average effect, not identical responses in every preparation.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 15:06–15:08 (2 minutes).**

**Say:** Pose the question: suppose there were no average treatment effect — how unusual would our estimate be? Invite predictions before the reveal. Keep the six observed differences and −10.4 estimate unchanged. Change only the mean effect in the simulation from −14 to zero. Biological effect SD remains 9, tube SD 3 and technical-reading SD 2.5; pairing, triplicate averaging and assay rounding remain. Positive and negative preparation effects can still occur. Do not name the null hypothesis yet. This is a hypothetical generating model, not a conclusion about compound Q.

**Conceptual point:** The no-average-effect situation is a concrete model for repeated experiments.

**Likely misconception:** No average effect means every preparation has zero response or no measurement variation.

**Optional follow-up:** Would all six changes be zero in every repetition?

**Sources:** Concepts adapted from AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 89–99, 106–114, 136, 142–146; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 50–55; DoctaMed.pdf pp. 30–39. Figures rebuilt; chance-language corrections follow CONTENT_MAP.md. R stats documentation, Student t distribution: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/TDist.html. The paired t calculation uses the six differences. Interpretation reference: ASA statement, https://www.amstat.org/asa/files/pdfs/p-valuestatement.pdf.

:::

## What would the no-effect model produce? {#build-null-distribution}

<div class="uncertainty-stack">
<img data-fragment-index="0" class="data-plot fragment fade-out" src="figures/generated/null-means-10.png" alt="Means from the first ten null experiments." />
<img data-fragment-index="0" class="data-plot fragment fade-in-then-out" src="figures/generated/null-means-100.png" alt="Means from the first hundred null experiments." />
<img data-fragment-index="1" class="data-plot fragment" src="figures/generated/null-means-10000.png" alt="Means from ten thousand no-average-effect experiments." />
</div>
<p class="takeaway fragment" data-fragment-index="2">The <strong>null distribution</strong> · H<sub>0</sub>: mean paired effect = 0</p>
<p class="fine">One entry = one experiment’s mean. Six new paired changes per experiment.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 15:08–15:11 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Accumulate 10, 100 and 10,000 means before naming the distribution on a final click. Define a null distribution as the distribution of the statistic across repeated experiments if the null hypothesis and model assumptions were true. Then name H0: the population mean paired effect is zero. The horizontal axis is in the same units, with the same 36-unit span and one-unit bins as the previous sampling-distribution sequence, now centered on zero. It is not a histogram of six observations and not a distribution of probabilities that hypotheses are true.

**Conceptual point:** The null distribution is the earlier sampling-distribution idea evaluated under a specified null model.

**Likely misconception:** H0 has been established by simulating from it, or each bar represents a different possible hypothesis.

**Optional follow-up:** What assumption produced the center of this histogram?

**Sources:** Concepts adapted from AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 89–99, 106–114, 136, 142–146; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 50–55; DoctaMed.pdf pp. 30–39. Figures rebuilt; chance-language corrections follow CONTENT_MAP.md. R stats documentation, Student t distribution: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/TDist.html. The paired t calculation uses the six differences. Interpretation reference: ASA statement, https://www.amstat.org/asa/files/pdfs/p-valuestatement.pdf.

:::

## How many standard errors away from zero? {#our-paired-t}

<img class="data-plot short-plot" src="figures/generated/null-se-steps.png" alt="Observed mean minus 10.4 and null zero, separated by about 2.10 steps of the estimated SE 4.96." />
<p class="takeaway">Our mean sits 2.1 SE steps below zero.</p>
<p class="medium">This distance, counted in SE steps, is called <strong>t</strong>. Here t = −2.10.</p>
<p class="small">Now we ask: how often would chance alone produce a result at least that far from zero?</p>

::: notes
**Time: 15:11–15:14 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Point to the figure. Zero is where no effect would sit. Our mean is 2.1 SE steps below it. That gap is what we need to judge — not the raw number, but how far it sits relative to the uncertainty in our estimate. Name it once: this SE-step distance is the t statistic, t = −2.10; it is the number software reports and the one you will see in papers. Negative means lower activity with Q; we will count distance in either direction. The question now is how often the null model would produce a result at least this far from zero. That is what the next slide answers.

**Conceptual point:** The standardized distance from zero is what the reference distribution compares against, not the raw mean.

**Likely misconception:** The test uses the SD of 36 technical readings, or a bigger raw mean always gives a smaller p-value regardless of SE.

**Optional follow-up:** If our SE had been 10 instead of 5, how many steps away would our mean be?

**Sources:** Concepts adapted from AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 89–99, 106–114, 136, 142–146; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 50–55; DoctaMed.pdf pp. 30–39.

:::

## How often would a result be at least this extreme? {#two-sided-p-value}

<img class="data-plot null-tail-plot" src="figures/generated/null-two-tails.png" alt="t distribution with both tails shaded beyond minus 2.10 and plus 2.10." />
<p class="null-definition">The p-value: if there were no true effect, how often would an experiment land at least as far from zero as ours — 2.1 SE steps, in either direction?</p>
<p class="takeaway fragment"><strong>Two-sided p = 0.090</strong> · both directions count</p>

::: notes
**Time: 15:14–15:17 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Point to the observed t at −2.10 and the equally distant +2.10 boundary. The question was about an average change in either direction, so add both tail probabilities. The actual paired t p-value is 0.08987058, rounded to 0.090. Under H0 and the assumptions, about 9% of repeated experiments produce absolute t at least 2.10. The simulation gives 9.07%, close to the analytical value; it is the standardized statistic, not the raw mean, being counted. Integrating the t distribution includes its entire infinite tails even though the plot shows only −5 to +5. Do not choose the direction after seeing a negative estimate.

**Conceptual point:** A p-value is a tail probability conditional on the null and statistical assumptions.

**Likely misconception:** The shaded area is the probability that H0 is true, or refers only to exactly the observed statistic.

**Optional follow-up:** Why does the right tail count when our observed estimate is negative?

**Sources:** Concepts adapted from AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 89–99, 106–114, 136, 142–146; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 50–55; DoctaMed.pdf pp. 30–39. Figures rebuilt; chance-language corrections follow CONTENT_MAP.md. R stats documentation, Student t distribution: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/TDist.html. The paired t calculation uses the six differences. Interpretation reference: ASA statement, https://www.amstat.org/asa/files/pdfs/p-valuestatement.pdf.

:::

## What does p = 0.090 mean? {#interpret-p-value .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Which statements are correct?</p>
<div class="null-options"><p>A · There is a 9% probability that H<sub>0</sub> is true.</p><p>B · There is a 9% probability that the result occurred by chance.</p><p>C · There is a 91% probability that the treatment really works.</p><p>D · A large p-value proves there is no effect.</p></div>
<div class="fragment"><p class="takeaway"><strong>All four are incorrect.</strong></p><p class="small">If there were no true effect, about 9% of repeated experiments would land at least 2.1 SE steps from zero.</p></div>
<p class="small fragment">B is close — but drops the condition. Repair: <em>"Assuming no true average effect, about 9% of repetitions produce a result at least this extreme."</em> Without that phrase, B implies the p-value assigns probability to H<sub>0</sub> being false — which it cannot do.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 15:17–15:21 (4 minutes).**

**Say:** Give one minute of individual choice and a minute of pair discussion, then reveal and debrief. All options reverse or distort the conditional statement. We assumed H0 to calculate the reference distribution; we did not calculate its probability. One minus p is not a probability that a compound works, and a large p does not prove zero effect.

On B specifically: it is the most seductive wrong answer and worth one extra minute. “By chance” sounds like it means “no real effect,” but that is exactly what we have not established. Results arise from random sampling whether or not there is a true effect — the question is only how often they are this extreme under H0. B drops the conditioning phrase, so it reads as if the p-value assigns a 9% probability to the null being true and a 91% probability to the treatment working — which is option C restated. Once participants add “assuming no true average effect,” B becomes approximately the correct statement. That addition is the whole point: the condition is not decorative, it is what makes the number mean anything.

**Conceptual point:** The probability is about possible data/statistics under an assumed model, not about the truth of that model.

**Likely misconception:** Subtracting p from one gives confidence that the treatment works.

**Optional follow-up:** Which phrase must appear before “about 9% of repeated experiments”?

**Sources:** Concepts adapted from AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 89–99, 106–114, 136, 142–146; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 50–55; DoctaMed.pdf pp. 30–39. Figures rebuilt; chance-language corrections follow CONTENT_MAP.md. R stats documentation, Student t distribution: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/TDist.html. The paired t calculation uses the six differences. Interpretation reference: ASA statement, https://www.amstat.org/asa/files/pdfs/p-valuestatement.pdf.

:::

## What does a 0.05 decision rule control? {#alpha-type-one}

<p class="medium">Pre-specify α = 0.05.<br>Reject H<sub>0</sub> when p &lt; 0.05.</p>
<img class="data-plot null-decision-plot" src="figures/generated/null-decisions.png" alt="First hundred null-model experiments shown as decisions; rust crosses reject the true null, teal dots do not." />
<div class="fragment"><p class="takeaway"><strong>Type I error:</strong> rejecting H<sub>0</sub> when H<sub>0</sub> is true</p><p class="small">About 5% in repeated use under H<sub>0</sub> and the model.</p></div>
<p class="fine">First 100 null repetitions, in order. Rust crosses: p &lt; 0.05. Across 10,000: 4.98%.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 15:21–15:24 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Only now introduce alpha as the prespecified decision threshold, a convention rather than a natural evidence boundary. A rejection under the chosen rule is often called statistically significant; that label does not establish biological importance. Every displayed experiment was generated with a true zero mean. Each rust cross is a rejection of a true H0, called a Type I error. There are not necessarily exactly five crosses in each block of 100; the first 100 are shown unselected. Across the same 10,000 null experiments 4.98% meet p<0.05. Under the ideal continuous normal model this rule’s long-run Type I rate is 5%; our rounded simulation approximates it. Alpha is not the probability that a particular conclusion is wrong, nor the proportion of all rejected claims that are false. A testing rule must be fixed in advance; do not retune it for the observed result.

**Conceptual point:** Alpha calibrates a repeated-use decision rule conditional on a true null, rather than labeling a universal evidence boundary.

**Likely misconception:** Every result with p<0.05 has a 5% probability of being a false finding.

**Optional follow-up:** Why can one hundred experiments show something other than exactly five crosses?

**Sources:** Concepts adapted from AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 89–99, 106–114, 136, 142–146; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 50–55; DoctaMed.pdf pp. 30–39. Figures rebuilt; chance-language corrections follow CONTENT_MAP.md. R stats documentation, Student t distribution: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/TDist.html. The paired t calculation uses the six differences. Interpretation reference: ASA statement, https://www.amstat.org/asa/files/pdfs/p-valuestatement.pdf.

:::

## Are these scientifically different? {#threshold-neighbours .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Two hypothetical results</p>
<div class="null-neighbours"><p>p = 0.049</p><p>p = 0.051</p></div>
<p class="takeaway fragment">A decision threshold does not create a jump in evidence.</p>
<p class="small">“Significant” and “not significant” cannot replace effect size, uncertainty or biological importance.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 15:24–15:26 (2 minutes).**

**Say:** Ask whether these values alone make the studies scientifically different. Under a prespecified p<0.05 rule the labels differ, but the data’s incompatibility with the null changes continuously rather than jumping at the cutoff. The comparison is only about nearby values for comparable analyses; p-values alone cannot rank very different experiments or scientific importance. A statistically significant result can be biologically small and does not guarantee replication. A result just above the convention does not establish no effect. Ask for estimates, intervals, design and biological context.

**Conceptual point:** A continuous compatibility summary and a threshold-based decision are different things.

**Likely misconception:** The p=0.049 study has discovered a real important effect and the p=0.051 study has found none.

**Optional follow-up:** What would you request before deciding which result matters biologically?

**Sources:** Concepts adapted from AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 89–99, 106–114, 136, 142–146; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 50–55; DoctaMed.pdf pp. 30–39. Figures rebuilt; chance-language corrections follow CONTENT_MAP.md. R stats documentation, Student t distribution: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/TDist.html. The paired t calculation uses the six differences. Interpretation reference: ASA statement, https://www.amstat.org/asa/files/pdfs/p-valuestatement.pdf.

:::

## A small p-value is not a large effect {#p-not-effect .key-message}

<p class="key-label">Key message</p>
<img class="data-plot short-plot" src="figures/generated/p-vs-effect.png" alt="Two hypothetical paired experiments with the same p-value of 0.01. Experiment A, 200 pairs: mean change minus 2 U/mg, narrow interval minus 3.5 to minus 0.5. Experiment B, 6 pairs: mean change minus 20 U/mg, wide interval minus 32.8 to minus 7.2." />
<p class="key-statement compact">Same p-value. Ten-fold different effect.</p>
<p class="key-support">p says how compatible the data are with zero — not how large or biologically relevant the change is. Judge relevance from the effect and its interval.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 15:26–15:27 (1 minute).**

**Say:** Point at the two p-values first: identical. Then at the two effects: −2 versus −20 U/mg. Experiment A has 200 pairs, so even a tiny change is estimated precisely and lies far from zero in SE steps. Experiment B has only six pairs, so a large change gives the same p. Ask which result matters biologically. A loss of 2 U/mg against roughly 98 U/mg is about 2% of activity; −20 is about 20%. The p-value cannot tell you this; the effect and its interval can. Both experiments are constructed illustrations, not L1 data.

**Conceptual point:** A p-value combines effect size, variability and sample size into one number. It does not measure magnitude or biological relevance.

**Likely misconception:** A smaller p-value means a larger or more important effect.

**Sources:** Constructed illustration; values derived exactly from p = 0.01 (scripts/generate_p_vs_effect.R). Wasserstein & Lazar (2016) *Am Stat* 70:129 — ASA statement on p-values, principle 5.
:::

## Break {#crc-break .break-slide}

<p class="big">30-minute break</p>
<p class="small keyline">Then: is the experiment big enough — and what happens with many outcomes?</p>

::: notes
**Time: 15:30–16:00 (30 minutes).**

**Say:** Pause for the full 30 minutes and resume at 16:00. Any time left before 15:30 is buffer for questions from the first part. Do not use the break to add teaching content.

**Conceptual point:** Preserve the break and attention for the second part.

**Likely misconception:** The scheduled break is optional overflow time.

**Optional follow-up:** No audience task during the break.

**Sources:** CRC205 schedule: 13:30–15:30, break, 16:00–18:30.
:::

## My p-value is 0.09. What should I do? {#p09-advice .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Give the researcher one piece of advice</p>
<img class="data-plot short-plot" src="figures/generated/null-ci-zero.png" alt="The unchanged mean paired effect minus 10.4 U/mg with 95 percent interval minus 23.2 to plus 2.3, including zero." />
<p class="takeaway"><strong>−10.4 U/mg</strong> · 95% CI <strong>−23.2 to +2.3</strong> · p = <strong>0.090</strong></p>
<p class="small">L1 · compound Q versus vehicle · six independent preparation pairs</p>

::: notes
**Time: 16:00–16:04 (4 minutes).**

**Say:** Let the audience advise a researcher who arrives after data collection wanting significance. Collect suggestions without classifying them yet: repeat, increase N, remove an outlier, another test, one-sided test, reduce variability, or conclude Q does not work. Spend two minutes collecting, one minute asking what information is missing, and one minute framing: why did this experiment not give a clear answer to the biological question? p=0.090 is not a failed experiment or a judgment on the researcher. The estimate and wide interval leave useful possibilities unresolved. These are the actual unchanged fictional Part 1 data. Keep the suggested actions visible on a board for the return later.

**Conceptual point:** An inconclusive result calls for interpretation and a scientific next step, not simply a smaller p-value.

**Likely misconception:** The immediate job of statistical advice is to make the current result cross 0.05.

**Optional follow-up:** What information would you request before recommending that action?

**Sources:** Adapted concepts: COURSE_OUTLINE.md sections 7–8; CONTENT_MAP.md flags on power and pairing; AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 92–95, 99, 137–148, 161–164, 187–192; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 56–62; DoctaMed.pdf pp. 37–42, 45–46. New figures from the documented L1 model. Calculation reference: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/power.t.test.html; two-sided rejection counts both tails.

:::

## Suppose the true mean effect is −14 U/mg {#specified-effect .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Predict · discuss with a neighbour</p>
<p class="medium">Same L1 protocol. Six new preparation pairs.<br>True mean effect fixed at <strong>−14 U/mg</strong>.</p>
<p class="takeaway">Would every repetition give p &lt; 0.05?</p>
<div class="fragment keyline"><p class="small">Same variability and paired t analysis.<br>Two-sided decision rule fixed in advance: p &lt; 0.05.</p></div>
<p class="fine">A teaching assumption from the original population model—not a conclusion from our p-value.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 16:04–16:06 (2 minutes).**

**Say:** Ask for a prediction before explaining. We return to the original generating model, whose mean −14 was fixed before its observed sample existed. It is not the observed estimate −10.4, not an estimate of truth derived from p, and not a validated minimum relevant effect. Each repetition creates six independent preparation changes with biological effect SD 9, tube SD 3 and triplicate technical SD 2.5; additive shared baselines cancel. The two-sided paired t rule is fixed at 0.05 for this illustration. It is not a mandatory rule for all science.

**Conceptual point:** Procedure performance can be evaluated under a specified nonzero effect, without claiming that effect is known in real data.

**Likely misconception:** The simulation has discovered that the real true effect is −14.

**Optional follow-up:** What varies across the repetitions if the true mean is fixed?

**Sources:** Adapted concepts: COURSE_OUTLINE.md sections 7–8; CONTENT_MAP.md flags on power and pairing; AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 92–95, 99, 137–148, 161–164, 187–192; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 56–62; DoctaMed.pdf pp. 37–42, 45–46. New figures from the documented L1 model. Calculation reference: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/power.t.test.html; two-sided rejection counts both tails.

:::

## Same biology, different experiments {#same-biology .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Inspect both experiments · 1 minute</p>
<img class="data-plot" src="figures/generated/power-examples.png" alt="Two simulated experiments each show six changes, their mean, 95 percent interval and p-value; one crosses 0.05 and one does not." />
<p class="takeaway">How can both arise from the same true mean effect?</p>
<p class="fine">Illustrative contrast: first rejection and first non-rejection selected from the simulation. Dashed line: true mean −14; solid line: 0.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 16:06–16:09 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Let participants inspect the two experiments for one minute. Dots are the six changes; the lower diamond is their mean and the line is its 95% interval. Repeat 1 has mean −16.4, CI −28.5 to −4.3, p=0.018. Repeat 8 has mean −9.5, CI −19.2 to +0.3, p=0.054. We deliberately selected the first experiment of each decision type to contrast outcomes; this pair does not estimate their frequencies. Both came from the same −14 population. Sampling variability changes the mean and estimated SD, so the threshold result can differ. Do not name power yet. A difference between labels is not evidence of a biological difference between the generating populations.

**Conceptual point:** Sampling variability can produce both rejection and non-rejection under the same nonzero average effect.

**Likely misconception:** One of the experiments must be wrong because their labels differ.

**Optional follow-up:** Which two ingredients of t changed between these experiments?

**Sources:** Adapted concepts: COURSE_OUTLINE.md sections 7–8; CONTENT_MAP.md flags on power and pairing; AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 92–95, 99, 137–148, 161–164, 187–192; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 56–62; DoctaMed.pdf pp. 37–42, 45–46. New figures from the documented L1 model. Calculation reference: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/power.t.test.html; two-sided rejection counts both tails.

:::

## What proportion would cross the threshold? {#power-as-frequency}

<img class="data-plot short-plot" src="figures/generated/power-decisions.png" alt="First one hundred repetitions from a true minus 14 population, with crosses for p below 0.05 and dots otherwise." />
<p class="takeaway fragment" data-fragment-index="0"><strong>78%</strong> crossed p &lt; 0.05 across 10,000 repetitions.</p>
<p class="small fragment" data-fragment-index="1"><strong>Power = P(reject H<sub>0</sub> | a specified alternative is true)</strong></p>
<p class="fine">Rust crosses reject; teal dots do not. First 100 shown in order; true mean −14 in every repetition.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 16:09–16:12 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Ask the audience to estimate the proportion of crosses, then reveal 78% across 10,000 trials. Only on the next click name statistical power. In plain language it is the long-run probability that this experiment and analysis will reject under a specified nonzero effect. It belongs to a full set of assumptions: effect, variability, independent N, design, alpha and analysis. The finite simulation gives 78%; the ideal normal paired-difference calculation gives about 76.9%, a Monte Carlo difference of about one percentage point. Do not present either as a guarantee that a particular replication succeeds. The crosses use the same decision symbols as Part 1, but the assumed truth is now nonzero; they are not Type I errors in this scenario. The first 100 are unselected; the illustrative pair from the previous slide is not the frequency denominator.

**Conceptual point:** Power is a repeated-experiment probability conditional on a specified alternative and procedure.

**Likely misconception:** Power is a fixed property of the named test, or the probability that an already observed result is true.

**Optional follow-up:** Which assumptions would you need to report alongside “about 78%”?

**Sources:** Adapted concepts: COURSE_OUTLINE.md sections 7–8; CONTENT_MAP.md flags on power and pairing; AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 92–95, 99, 137–148, 161–164, 187–192; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 56–62; DoctaMed.pdf pp. 37–42, 45–46. New figures from the documented L1 model. Calculation reference: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/power.t.test.html; two-sided rejection counts both tails.

:::

## p > α does not mean no effect {#no-effect-fallacy .key-message}

<p class="key-label">Key message</p>

<p class="big">Our interval: −23 to +2 U/mg.</p>
<p class="big">It includes zero — and a reduction<br>of almost a quarter of enzyme activity.</p>
<p class="key-statement compact keyline">Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 16:12–16:13 (1 minute).**

**Say:** State this once, clearly, and move on. The interval covers zero — that is why p exceeds α. But it also covers biologically meaningful reductions: −23 U/mg against a vehicle mean of about 98 U/mg is a loss of roughly 24% of activity. A non-significant result from this experiment cannot distinguish "no effect" from "an effect we lacked the power to see." Do not open a discussion.

**Conceptual point:** A wide interval that includes zero is compatible with many effect sizes, including large ones. Non-rejection is not confirmation of the null.

**Likely misconception:** p > 0.05 means the treatment has no effect, or the null hypothesis is true.

**Optional follow-up:** None — this is a statement, not a discussion.

**Sources:** Altman & Bland (1995) *BMJ* 311:1600 — "Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence."
:::

## What would change that proportion? {#power-factors}

<p class="prompt-tag">Predict each change before the next reveal</p>
<div class="uncertainty-stack">
<img data-fragment-index="0" class="data-plot fragment fade-in-then-out" src="figures/generated/power-factor-1.png" alt="Larger true effect magnitude gives higher power, other assumptions fixed." />
<img data-fragment-index="1" class="data-plot fragment fade-in-then-out" src="figures/generated/power-factor-2.png" alt="Greater biological response SD gives lower power, other assumptions fixed." />
<img data-fragment-index="2" class="data-plot fragment fade-in-then-out" src="figures/generated/power-factor-3.png" alt="More independent preparation pairs give higher power, other assumptions fixed." />
<img data-fragment-index="3" class="data-plot fragment " src="figures/generated/power-factor-4.png" alt="A more stringent smaller alpha gives lower power, other assumptions fixed." />
</div>
<p class="fine">Vary one assumption at a time: effect, biological variability, independent N, then alpha. Other settings stay fixed.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 16:13–16:17 (4 minutes).**

**Say:** Use four short predictions, one before each reveal. Larger true effect moves estimates further from zero; lower biological variability narrows their distribution; larger independent N lowers SE. A smaller alpha lowers the long-run Type I rate but also lowers power, all else fixed. Baseline is effect magnitude 14, n=6, biological-effect SD 9, tube SD 3, technical SD 2.5 with three aliquots, and two-sided alpha 0.05. The variability curve changes only biological-effect SD and retains the measurement components. These curves use exact noncentral-t probabilities under independent normal differences, counting both tails. No derivation is needed. Do not recommend loosening alpha to rescue the observed p-value; it is a prospective decision setting.

**Conceptual point:** Power changes when the assumed effect, variability or procedure changes.

**Likely misconception:** One quoted power number applies regardless of effect size, design or decision rule.

**Optional follow-up:** Which of these can you improve through experimental design rather than wishful thinking?

**Sources:** Adapted concepts: COURSE_OUTLINE.md sections 7–8; CONTENT_MAP.md flags on power and pairing; AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 92–95, 99, 137–148, 161–164, 187–192; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 56–62; DoctaMed.pdf pp. 37–42, 45–46. New figures from the documented L1 model. Calculation reference: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/power.t.test.html; two-sided rejection counts both tails.

:::

## What effect is worth detecting? {#minimum-relevant-effect .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Decide · then defend your threshold</p>
<div class="research-paths"><div><h3>What we observed</h3><p>−10.4 U/mg<br>from six preparations</p></div><div><h3>What would matter</h3><p>A minimum relevant effect<br>justified by the biology</p></div></div>
<p class="takeaway">“How many replicates?” comes after “What question must they answer?”</p>

::: notes
**Time: 16:17–16:21 (4 minutes).**

**Say:** Ask participants to describe how they would decide whether an enzyme-activity reduction matters: downstream biology, assay reliability, prior evidence or a decision to proceed.
