The observed effect is a noisy estimate from a small sample; it is not automatically the truth to plug into planning. The teaching mean −14 is likewise not an established relevant threshold. Specify a minimum relevant effect on the same U/mg scale and within the defined L1 conditions. Planning detects a departure from zero assuming an effect of that size; it does not prove an effect exceeds the relevance boundary. No numeric biological threshold is invented.

**Conceptual point:** Prospective planning needs a scientifically motivated effect, not an uncritical reuse of a small observed estimate.

**Likely misconception:** A sample-size calculation should use −10.4 simply because that is our pilot mean.

**Optional follow-up:** What evidence would justify calling a given change biologically meaningful?

**Sources:** Adapted concepts: COURSE_OUTLINE.md sections 7–8; CONTENT_MAP.md flags on power and pairing; AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 92–95, 99, 137–148, 161–164, 187–192; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 56–62; DoctaMed.pdf pp. 37–42, 45–46. New figures from the documented L1 model. Calculation reference: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/power.t.test.html; two-sided rejection counts both tails.

:::

## Can a better comparison remove irrelevant variation? {#pairing-design}

<img class="data-plot" src="figures/generated/power-design.png" alt="Sampling distributions for six compound and six vehicle cultures from unrelated preparations versus six matched split preparations, both with twelve assigned culture tubes." />
<p class="takeaway">Shared preparation variation cancels in a meaningful paired contrast.</p>
<p class="fine">Same 12 culture tubes, true mean −14 and balanced conditions across days. Pairing must reflect a real shared source.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 16:21–16:24 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Compare twelve unrelated preparations, six per condition, with six independent preparations split into twelve tubes. Both layouts balance conditions across days, so this comparison isolates matching instead of deliberately confounding treatment with day. Unrelated preparation baselines vary with SD 15 and no longer cancel within contrasts; the mean estimate’s simulated SE is about 9.6 instead of 4.2 U/mg. Both use three assay readings per tube and the same treatment effect process. Randomization is still within the relevant allocation structure. Pairing is useful because matching captures a positively shared baseline; it is not automatically better for arbitrary pairs or every cost/covariance structure. Measuring all controls on unrelated control-only days would add possible confounding, which statistics cannot remove by increasing N. This figure compares estimator precision, not a menu of tests or proof that every paired design is superior.

**Conceptual point:** Meaningful pairing and balanced blocking can reduce irrelevant variation before analysis.

**Likely misconception:** Any post-hoc pairing improves precision, or pairing replaces randomization and day balance.

**Optional follow-up:** What feature makes the two tubes from one preparation a meaningful pair?

**Sources:** Adapted concepts: COURSE_OUTLINE.md sections 7–8; CONTENT_MAP.md flags on power and pairing; AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 92–95, 99, 137–148, 161–164, 187–192; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 56–62; DoctaMed.pdf pp. 37–42, 45–46. New figures from the documented L1 model. Calculation reference: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/power.t.test.html; two-sided rejection counts both tails.

:::

## Where should six additional assay wells go? {#six-more-wells .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Choose, then explain what your choice buys</p>
<div class="fragment"><img class="data-plot short-plot" src="figures/generated/power-wells.png" alt="Under this model, six extra technical assay wells barely change SE; one new independent pair, measured in six wells, reduces SE more." /></div>
<p class="small">Technical repeats improve measurement precision and assay checks.<br>New preparations add information about population responses.</p>
<p class="fine">42 assay wells in either option. A new pair also requires new culture work; total costs are not equal.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 16:24–16:27 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Make the resource unit explicit: assay wells, not culture tubes. Current design uses 36 readings. Option A adds one assay reading to each tube in three existing pairs, six additional technical readings. Option B adds one independent preparation split into two tubes, with three readings each, also six assay wells. A reduces SE to 99.7% of baseline; B to about 92.6%. In this model response variation dominates, so independent replication brings more information about the population mean. The numerical comparison concerns precision, not applying an unmodified t calibration to unequal technical counts. Technical replication is useful for measurement precision and assay reliability, especially when technical error is substantial; its value depends on the components and total costs. Option B requires preparation and culture resources beyond assay wells. Never call technical replicates independent biological units.

**Conceptual point:** Replication choices should follow the source of uncertainty and the resource being counted.

**Likely misconception:** Technical repeats are useless, or six extra readings necessarily mean six extra independent responses.

**Optional follow-up:** If technical noise dominated or new cultures were much more expensive, how would you reassess the options?

**Sources:** Adapted concepts: COURSE_OUTLINE.md sections 7–8; CONTENT_MAP.md flags on power and pairing; AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 92–95, 99, 137–148, 161–164, 187–192; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 56–62; DoctaMed.pdf pp. 37–42, 45–46. New figures from the documented L1 model. Calculation reference: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/power.t.test.html; two-sided rejection counts both tails.

:::

## How many pairs does your experiment need? {#planning-sensitivity .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Find your experiment's number in the grid</p>
<img class="data-plot" src="figures/generated/power-sensitivity.png" alt="Required independent pairs across effect magnitudes 6, 10 and 14 and difference SDs 8, 12 and 16, with power target 80 percent and two-sided alpha 0.05." />
<p class="takeaway">Numbers are required <strong>independent preparation pairs</strong>.</p>
<p class="fine">Illustrative assumptions: paired t analysis, 80% target, two-sided α = 0.05. These are conventions, not requirements or an L1 recommendation.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 16:27–16:30 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Use the grid rather than announcing one N. For assumed effect magnitude 10 and paired-change SD 12, the smallest integer N meeting 80% is 14 completed pairs. With effect 6 and SD 16 it is 58; with effect 14 and SD 8 it is 5. The grid uses the normal independent paired-difference model and counts both rejection tails. Eighty percent is a common planning convention, not a universal standard; neither is alpha 0.05 mandatory. The effect and SD values are illustrative scenarios, not validated biological relevance thresholds or confidence bounds from this pilot. If assumptions are wrong, achieved performance changes. Report them, examine sensitivity and consider credible external or pilot variance information without trusting one noisy point estimate. These values exclude attrition, operational block constraints and model misspecification.

**Conceptual point:** Required N is conditional on assumptions, not a certificate of adequate design.

**Likely misconception:** Meeting a calculated N guarantees a decisive result or replication.

**Optional follow-up:** Which assumptions would you want to defend before choosing one of these numbers?

**Sources:** Adapted concepts: COURSE_OUTLINE.md sections 7–8; CONTENT_MAP.md flags on power and pairing; AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 92–95, 99, 137–148, 161–164, 187–192; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 56–62; DoctaMed.pdf pp. 37–42, 45–46. New figures from the documented L1 model. Calculation reference: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/power.t.test.html; two-sided rejection counts both tails.

:::

## My p-value is 0.09. What should I do now? {#advice-revisited .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Revise your earlier advice · 1 minute</p>
<div class="research-paths"><div><h3>Inform the next experiment</h3><p class="small">Interpret the effect and interval.<br>Replicate independently if justified.<br>Improve design and reduce avoidable variation.<br>Plan independent N and analysis in advance.</p></div><div><h3>Do not chase the threshold</h3><p class="small">Switch analysis only to get p &lt; 0.05.<br>Delete observations just for a smaller p.<br>Choose one-sided after seeing direction.<br>Keep adding samples until p crosses.</p></div></div>

::: notes
**Time: 16:30–16:33 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Return to the audience’s original suggestions and let them revise one. Interpretation, acknowledging uncertainty, an independent replication if justified, better design, reduced avoidable variation and prospective biological replication are defensible directions. A method may need correction if scientifically or diagnostically inappropriate, and exclusions can be justified by an established QC rule; changing choices solely for significance is different and requires transparent handling rather than result shopping. Do not choose a one-sided question after seeing the direction or keep adding observations until a threshold appears. Establish the principle only; the later block will address flexible analysis in detail. Neither high power guarantees replication nor low planned power automatically invalidates a significant result. Evaluate design, assumptions, effect, interval and reporting.

**Conceptual point:** Prospective improvements serve the scientific question; post-hoc threshold chasing does not resolve it.

**Likely misconception:** A different test or selectively reduced dataset is an appropriate fix because it produces a smaller p-value.

**Optional follow-up:** Which original suggestion would you keep, and how would you make it prospective?

**Sources:** Adapted concepts: COURSE_OUTLINE.md sections 7–8; CONTENT_MAP.md flags on power and pairing; AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 92–95, 99, 137–148, 161–164, 187–192; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 56–62; DoctaMed.pdf pp. 37–42, 45–46. New figures from the documented L1 model. Calculation reference: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/power.t.test.html; two-sided rejection counts both tails.

:::

## We measured 20 outcomes. One gave p = 0.03. {#one-among-twenty .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">The L1 experiment now measures 20 markers</p>
<p class="big">Is p = 0.03 still p = 0.03?</p>
<p class="takeaway fragment">The individual number is unchanged.<br>The opportunity to find a small number has changed.</p>
<p class="fine">Hypothetical expansion of the assay—not a revision of the observed enzyme result, p = 0.090.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 16:33–16:35 (2 minutes).**

**Say:** Ask for an answer before revealing the distinction. The raw p-value still describes its particular test under that test's assumptions. But finding a small result after twenty chances is a different event from a single preselected comparison. State the central question aloud: how many chances did we give ourselves to find something? This is a hypothetical expanded L1 protocol; the original enzyme result has not been changed to 0.03. No correction method is needed yet.

**Conceptual point:** A valid individual p-value and the interpretation of a selected finding across many tests are different questions.

**Likely misconception:** Multiplicity changes the measured raw p-value, or its numerical validity removes the need to consider selection.

**Optional follow-up:** Would your answer change if this marker had been the sole prespecified primary outcome?

**Sources:** Concepts adapted from CONTENT_MAP.md section 9 and review register: AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 78–80, 167–173, 178–184; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 63–70; DoctaMed.pdf p. 44. Figures rebuilt, not copied. Method reference: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/p.adjust.html (Holm strong FWER control; BH FDR and dependence caveats).

:::

## How many chances did we give ourselves? {#twenty-chances .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Predict: how many experiments find at least one?</p>
<div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="0"><img class="data-plot short-plot" src="figures/generated/multi-families.png" alt="First hundred all-null families; crosses indicate at least one raw p below 0.05." /></div>
<p class="takeaway fragment" data-fragment-index="0"><strong>64.27%</strong> of 10,000 experiments found at least one.</p>
<p class="small fragment" data-fragment-index="1">Under independence: 1 − (1 − 0.05)<sup>20</sup> ≈ 0.64</p>
<p class="fine">One symbol = one 20-test experiment. A 5% per-test rate is not a 5% any-error rate.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 16:35–16:38 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Collect predictions before revealing the grid. Crosses mean at least one of twenty null tests crossed 0.05; the first hundred families are unselected. Across all 10,000, 64.27% had one or more. On the next click show the independence calculation: the probability none crosses is .95 to the twentieth power, so its complement is about .6415. Emphasize that this exact formula requires independent tests with exact .05 marginal size. Correlated valid marker tests do not generally have this same probability. Distinguish the per-test probability from the chance of any false rejection across a family; an expected false count is a third quantity, introduced later.

**Conceptual point:** Many opportunities amplify the probability of at least one Type I error across the collection.

**Likely misconception:** Twenty tests at 5% means a 5% chance of any false finding, or necessarily one error every time.

**Optional follow-up:** Which assumption allowed us to multiply the twenty no-error probabilities?

**Sources:** Concepts adapted from CONTENT_MAP.md section 9 and review register: AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 78–80, 167–173, 178–184; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 63–70; DoctaMed.pdf p. 44. Figures rebuilt, not copied. Method reference: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/p.adjust.html (Holm strong FWER control; BH FDR and dependence caveats).

:::

## Which claims belong to the same family? {#define-family .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">What shared claim would make these one family?</p>
<p class="medium"><strong>Family-wise error rate (FWER)</strong></p>
<p class="takeaway">Probability of at least one Type I error within a defined family of hypotheses</p>
<div class="definitions-pair"><p class="small">20 prespecified cytokines<br>Several treatment contrasts</p><p class="small">Multiple time points<br>Several primary endpoints</p></div>
<p class="fine">The family follows the scientific claims and decision—not whichever results look interesting.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 16:38–16:40 (2 minutes).**

**Say:** Only now name FWER. It is a probability that any true null in a defined family is rejected, even if some other hypotheses in that family are false. Ask which outcomes contribute to the same intended claim or decision. Twenty cytokines for one question may form a family; so might several contrasts, time points or primary endpoints. Scientific context and the promised error protection determine the family; there is not one uniquely correct grouping independent of purpose. Define it prospectively where possible, not after seeing which grouping gives a favorable result.

**Conceptual point:** FWER control requires an interpretable scientific family of claims.

**Likely misconception:** A family is automatically every column in a file, or can be chosen after looking at p-values solely to keep a finding.

**Optional follow-up:** What shared claim would make our twenty L1 markers one family?

**Sources:** Concepts adapted from CONTENT_MAP.md section 9 and review register: AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 78–80, 167–173, 178–184; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 63–70; DoctaMed.pdf p. 44. Figures rebuilt, not copied. Method reference: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/p.adjust.html (Holm strong FWER control; BH FDR and dependence caveats).

:::

## What if we measured 20,000 genes? {#twenty-thousand}

<img class="data-plot short-plot" src="figures/generated/multi-genes.png" alt="Two hundred dots represent twenty thousand genes; ten rust dots represent the expected one thousand raw false positives." />
<p class="takeaway">20,000 × 0.05 = <strong>1,000 expected raw false positives</strong></p>
<p class="fine">All nulls true; valid exact 5% tests. Each dot represents 100 genes. Illustration of an expectation—not one observed screen.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 16:40–16:42 (2 minutes).**

**Say:** Change scale to an exploratory transcriptome-wide screen. Under twenty thousand true nulls, the expected number of raw p-values below .05 is one thousand. Expectation is a repeated-run average, not an exact count in one screen. This expected-count calculation uses linearity of expectation and does not require independent tests if each marginal size is .05; valid conservative tests give at most that expectation. Under independence the probability of at least one is essentially one, a different quantity from the expected count. The dot display depicts the expectation rather than an invented RNA-seq dataset or software output. Protecting against even one error may be demanding for candidate discovery, motivating a different scientific goal.

**Conceptual point:** The expected count of false positives is distinct from the probability of any false positive.

**Likely misconception:** A thousand expected errors means a thousand must occur in this dataset, or it is itself a probability.

**Optional follow-up:** Would a candidate screen and a small set of primary confirmatory outcomes need the same promise?

**Sources:** Concepts adapted from CONTENT_MAP.md section 9 and review register: AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 78–80, 167–173, 178–184; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 63–70; DoctaMed.pdf p. 44. Figures rebuilt, not copied. Method reference: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/p.adjust.html (Holm strong FWER control; BH FDR and dependence caveats).

:::

## What error promise fits a discovery list? {#introduce-fdr}

<p class="small">New simulation: 4 nonzero marker effects + 16 true nulls; independent tests.</p>
<img class="data-plot multi-short" src="figures/generated/multi-fdp.png" alt="False-discovery proportions across the first eighty mixed-truth screens; the mean across ten thousand is about 4.1 percent." />
<p class="takeaway"><strong>FDR:</strong> expected false-discovery proportion over repeated use</p>
<p class="fine">Line: mean false fraction 4.1% across 10,000 screens. No discoveries → fraction 0.<br>One dataset's fraction is not guaranteed to equal the target.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 16:42–16:44 (2 minutes).**

**Say:** Contrast the scientific aim of avoiding even one false confirmatory claim with producing a candidate list for follow-up. Name FDR only after posing the list question. FDR is the expected proportion of false discoveries among all discoveries; if there are no discoveries, the fraction is zero by convention. The first eighty BH-controlled screens show variable realized fractions; the teal line marks the mean across ten thousand, about 4.1%. FDR 5% is not a guarantee about this list — it is a repeated-use expectation. A realized list can have zero, a large fraction, or even all false discoveries. In real science we do not know which specific claims are false. The concept of a fraction rather than a count is the take-home.

**Conceptual point:** FDR is a repeated-procedure expectation of a fraction, not a known fraction in one observed discovery set.

**Likely misconception:** At 5% FDR exactly 5% of this study's significant genes are false.

**Optional follow-up:** Why must a run with no discoveries still have a defined fraction?

**Sources:** Concepts adapted from CONTENT_MAP.md section 9 and review register: AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 78–80, 167–173, 178–184; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 63–70; DoctaMed.pdf p. 44. Figures rebuilt, not copied. Method reference: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/p.adjust.html (Holm strong FWER control; BH FDR and dependence caveats).

:::

## Which promise does the scientific question need? {#fwer-versus-fdr}

<div class="research-paths"><div><h3>Confirmatory family</h3><p class="small">How likely is even one false rejection?<br><strong>FWER</strong></p></div><div><h3>Exploratory candidate list</h3><p class="small">What false fraction is controlled on average?<br><strong>FDR</strong></p></div></div>
<p class="takeaway">Choose the error criterion from the scientific purpose.</p>
<p class="fine">In our mixed simulation, controlling FDR kept the average false fraction at 4.1% — but at least one false hit still occurred in 10.2% of screens.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 16:44–16:46 (2 minutes).**

**Say:** Compare promises rather than declaring a winning correction. A few prespecified primary outcomes may need strong protection against any false claim. A transcriptome-wide candidate screen with independent confirmation planned may prioritize a controlled expected false fraction. In the mixed simulation BH gives FDR 4.13% and FWER 10.16%; those are different denominators and summaries, not contradictory results. These realized rates are model-specific, not guarantees for all datasets. Error control does not establish biological importance; keep magnitude, uncertainty and validation in view.

**Conceptual point:** FWER and FDR address different scientific commitments.

**Likely misconception:** A procedure controlling FDR at 5% must also control the chance of any false rejection at 5%.

**Optional follow-up:** Which promise would you make for a primary claim that determines whether a compound advances?

**Sources:** Concepts adapted from CONTENT_MAP.md section 9 and review register: AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 78–80, 167–173, 178–184; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 63–70; DoctaMed.pdf p. 44. Figures rebuilt, not copied. Method reference: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/p.adjust.html (Holm strong FWER control; BH FDR and dependence caveats).

:::

## You report p = 0.03. What else did you try? {#what-else-tried .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Name one hidden opportunity from your own work</p>
<div class="multi-choices"><p class="fragment">20 endpoints</p><p class="fragment">Several doses</p><p class="fragment">Several time points</p><p class="fragment">Several subgroups</p><p class="fragment">Different exclusion rules</p><p class="fragment">Transformed or untransformed outcome</p><p class="fragment">Paired or unpaired analysis</p><p class="fragment">One-sided or two-sided test</p><p class="fragment">Stopping or adding observations after a look</p></div>
<p class="takeaway">Multiple opportunities can be visible—or hidden in analytical choices.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 16:46–16:49 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Reveal the choices one at a time and invite examples. Multiplicity can come from planned parallel tests and from decisions affected by observed outcomes. The opportunities are not interchangeable: paired versus unpaired must follow design; transformations and exclusions can be scientifically justified; stopping rules change the sampling procedure. Do not automatically apply a simple Bonferroni count to every option on this slide. The issue is what full selection process produced the reported analysis and whether its claimed error guarantee accounts for that process. Avoid moralizing: thoughtful analysts can create a data-dependent path without deliberate threshold chasing.

**Conceptual point:** The inferential context includes analytical flexibility, not just the number of outcome columns.

**Likely misconception:** Reporting only one test removes the problem, or every analysis choice can be repaired by counting commands.

**Optional follow-up:** Which choices were fixed by the experimental design, and which could have changed after seeing results?

**Sources:** Concepts adapted from CONTENT_MAP.md section 9 and review register: AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 78–80, 167–173, 178–184; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 63–70; DoctaMed.pdf p. 44. Figures rebuilt, not copied. Method reference: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/p.adjust.html (Holm strong FWER control; BH FDR and dependence caveats).

:::

## The test direction must be specified before seeing the data {#one-sided-after-peeking}

<div class="research-paths">
<div><h3>Planned one-sided</h3><p class="small">Direction fixed before collection: only a reduction is biologically plausible.</p><p class="small">α = 0.05 on one tail. Legitimate.</p></div>
<div><h3>Post-hoc one-sided</h3><p class="small">Direction chosen after seeing the effect is negative: "clearly it's a reduction, so one-sided."</p><p class="small">Two-sided p = 0.090 → one-sided p = 0.045. The α = 0.05 promise was not what was kept.</p></div>
</div>
<p class="takeaway">Choosing the direction after looking is a hidden extra test.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 16:49–16:51 (2 minutes).**

**Say:** The one-sided versus two-sided decision must be made before the data are examined, not after. For the L1 experiment: two-sided p is 0.090. If you look at the data, observe the negative sign, and then decide to use a one-sided test, you obtain p = 0.045 — just across the threshold. But you used the data twice: once to choose the direction, and once to compute the p-value. The effective α is no longer 0.05. The test is legitimate only if the direction was fixed before collection on scientific grounds — for example, if a positive enzyme increase from a kinase inhibitor is mechanistically impossible and would not be reported regardless of size. That constraint must be documented before the experiment. Retrospective justification ("of course we only expected a reduction") is not equivalent.

**Conceptual point:** A p-value guarantees its stated error rate only when the procedure — including the direction — is fully pre-specified. Post-hoc direction choice changes the effective procedure.

**Likely misconception:** Choosing one-sided because the observed direction is "biologically obvious in hindsight" is a legitimate scientific justification.

**Optional follow-up:** How would you document a pre-specified one-sided decision in a lab notebook entry written before the experiment?

**Sources:** Bland & Altman (1994) *BMJ* 309:248 — one-tailed vs two-tailed significance; Vaux (2012) *Nature* 492:180.
:::

## Exploration is useful science {#explore-then-confirm .key-message}

<p class="key-label">Key message</p>

<p class="medium">Explore → generate a hypothesis<br>→ independently test it</p>
<p class="key-statement compact">A p-value from exploratory data means little:<br>the hypothesis came from the same data.</p>
<p class="key-support">Show which ideas emerged from the data — and test them in a new experiment.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 16:51–16:53 (2 minutes).**

**Say:** Reconnect to Part 1. Transformations, subgroup inspection and hypothesis generation are legitimate exploratory work. The problem is attaching confirmatory error guarantees as though the hypothesis and analysis had been fixed before those same observations were examined. Report discovery as discovery and independently test important resulting claims with an appropriate design. Independence means genuinely new information not reused to select the claim; it does not guarantee success. Avoid suggesting that every exploratory calculation needs a mechanical adjustment or that exploration is inferior science. Land the key message: when the hypothesis was suggested by the same data, a p-value from those data has almost no evidential value — it describes how unusual the pattern was that we already selected for being unusual. Show the exploration; reserve testing for the new experiment.

**Conceptual point:** Exploration and confirmation serve complementary roles with different inferential claims.

**Likely misconception:** Trying multiple ideas is intrinsically illegitimate, or relabeling the same analysis makes it independent confirmation.

**Optional follow-up:** What would you carry forward from a promising marker screen into a new experiment?

**Sources:** Concepts adapted from CONTENT_MAP.md section 9 and review register: AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 78–80, 167–173, 178–184; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 63–70; DoctaMed.pdf p. 44. Figures rebuilt, not copied. Method reference: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/p.adjust.html (Holm strong FWER control; BH FDR and dependence caveats).

:::

## What does the reader learn from these two reports? {#selective-reporting .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Compare reports A and B · 1 minute</p>
<div class="research-paths"><div><h3>Report A</h3><p class="small">"Outcome X was significantly affected, p = 0.03."</p></div><div><h3>Report B</h3><p class="small">"We examined 20 prespecified outcomes. X had raw p = 0.03; the full family, effect estimates, intervals and planned multiplicity analysis are reported."</p></div></div>
<p class="takeaway">Same raw p-value. A different view of how it was found.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 16:53–16:56 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Allow a minute to compare reports and two to discuss. Imagine twenty measured outcomes, nineteen without a small p and one p=.03. Report A hides that context. Report B tells the reader what the family was and makes the full results available; it must actually provide the named estimates and analysis, not merely claim transparency. If Bonferroni on twenty was the plan, .03 becomes .60; other strategies depend on the specified purpose. Reporting all outcomes does not itself correct invalid inference, but concealing them prevents assessment. Distinguish raw from adjusted p-values and ordinary from multiplicity-aware intervals. Do not describe the nineteen as proof that those markers have no effect.

**Conceptual point:** Transparent reporting of outcomes and selection is necessary for interpreting the reported result.

**Likely misconception:** A selected p=.03 tells the complete story, or a transparency sentence alone repairs the statistical analysis.

**Optional follow-up:** What information in Report B changes your interpretation of the same number?

**Sources:** Concepts adapted from CONTENT_MAP.md section 9 and review register: AppliedStats_2026.pdf pp. 78–80, 167–173, 178–184; Stats_PhD_MR_CVS_2024.pdf pp. 63–70; DoctaMed.pdf p. 44. Figures rebuilt, not copied. Method reference: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/p.adjust.html (Holm strong FWER control; BH FDR and dependence caveats).

:::

## Which statistical test should I use? {#test-name-late .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">What information is missing?</p>
<div class="tests-grid">
<p class="fragment">Biological question?</p><p class="fragment">Experimental unit?</p><p class="fragment">Measured outcome?</p><p class="fragment">Comparison of interest?</p><p class="fragment">Related observations?</p><p class="fragment">Experimental design?</p></div>
<p class="takeaway fragment">The name of the test comes late.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 16:56–16:59 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Give pairs a minute to request information before revealing the six prompts one at a time. Take two suggestions and ask what each would change. A spreadsheet and a software menu do not specify the experiment. Do not answer with a test yet.

**Conceptual point:** Analysis starts with the scientific question and data-generating design.

**Likely misconception:** The number of columns identifies the correct test.

**Optional follow-up:** What could two identical spreadsheets conceal about their designs?

**Sources:** Rebuilt using CONTENT_MAP.md concepts: experimental units and pairing (A pp. 121–144), models and assumptions (A pp. 115–160), design and sampling (R pp. 45–62), and prospective planning (D pp. 45–46, 52). Numerical examples are newly generated or explicitly reuse the original L1 data. Method checks: official R t.test, lm and wilcox.test documentation; see SESSION2_TESTS_NOTES.md.
:::

## 120 cells. What is N? {#rows-and-units .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">What is missing from the row count?</p>
<div class="tests-chain">Donors? → cultures → wells → cells</div>
<p class="question">Where was Q assigned?<br>Which units were independently generated?</p>
<p class="takeaway fragment">The row count cannot answer this.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 16:59–17:01 (2 minutes).**

**Say:** Deliberately withhold counts at the higher levels. Allow a short discussion before explaining that a single N can hide several levels: assignment units, sampled donors, cultures, wells and cells. Request identities, allocation, pooling and shared batches. If Q was assigned to cultures, cells are subsamples; if wells were assigned within cultures, the design is blocked or clustered rather than simply 120 independent cells. The model must reflect where independent information enters.

**Conceptual point:** Dependence cannot be reconstructed from row count alone.

**Likely misconception:** Calling every measured cell a biological replicate makes it independent.

**Optional follow-up:** What metadata would let us reconstruct the hierarchy?

**Sources:** Rebuilt using CONTENT_MAP.md concepts: experimental units and pairing (A pp. 121–144), models and assumptions (A pp. 115–160), design and sampling (R pp. 45–62), and prospective planning (D pp. 45–46, 52). Numerical examples are newly generated or explicitly reuse the original L1 data. Method checks: official R t.test, lm and wilcox.test documentation; see SESSION2_TESTS_NOTES.md.
:::

## Metadata decide the analysis {#metadata-matters .key-message}

<p class="key-label">Key message</p>
<p class="key-statement">Record preparation, day, tube and well<br>for every value.</p>
<p class="key-support">Without metadata nobody — including you in six months — can reconstruct the design, find N, or choose the right analysis.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 17:01–17:02 (1 minute).**

**Say:** The previous slide could not be answered from the row count, only from metadata. For every measured value, record which preparation, culture or donor it came from, the day or batch, the treated tube or well, and the technical replicate number. Add plate positions, passage numbers, reagent lots and any exclusion with its reason. This costs minutes at the bench and is impossible to recover later. It is also what lets a statistician — or a reviewer — check pairing, blocking and pseudoreplication.

**Conceptual point:** The correct analysis follows the data-generating structure, which only metadata preserve.

**Likely misconception:** Metadata are administrative detail; the measured values alone are the data.

**Sources:** Lazic (2010) *BMC Neurosci* 11:5 — pseudoreplication; Wilkinson et al. (2016) *Sci Data* 3:160018 — FAIR principles.
:::

## Same measurements. Same analysis? {#same-columns-different-design}

<div class="tests-grid"><p><strong>A</strong> Six control cultures + six unrelated Q cultures</p><p><strong>B</strong> Six preparations, each split into control and Q</p></div><img class="data-plot tests-plot" src="figures/generated/tests-design-ci.png" alt="Identical observed group values yield different intervals under independent and paired design assumptions." /><p class="takeaway">The spreadsheet columns do not tell us the design.</p>
<p class="fine">Counterfactual comparison using the same values. The actual L1 experiment is B.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 17:02–17:05 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Have the audience predict whether the mean difference or its uncertainty changes. Both analyses give −10.4. Under unrelated-culture assumptions the Welch interval is −33.6 to 12.8; under the actual paired design it is −23.2 to 2.3. This is a counterfactual illustration, not permission to choose the narrower result. Positive within-pair association removes shared variation here. Pairing does not universally improve precision; covariance and the cost/design context matter. Choose the procedure from provenance before inspecting which gives a preferred answer.

**Conceptual point:** Dependence changes the uncertainty calculation even with identical marginal values.

**Likely misconception:** Try both and retain whichever is significant.

**Optional follow-up:** Which fact in the laboratory notebook decides between A and B?

**Sources:** Rebuilt using CONTENT_MAP.md concepts: experimental units and pairing (A pp. 121–144), models and assumptions (A pp. 115–160), design and sampling (R pp. 45–62), and prospective planning (D pp. 45–46, 52). Numerical examples are newly generated or explicitly reuse the original L1 data. Method checks: official R t.test, lm and wilcox.test documentation; see SESSION2_TESTS_NOTES.md.
:::

## Pairing and blocking buy power {#paired-design-power .key-message}

<p class="key-label">Key message</p>
<p class="key-statement">Paired and blocked designs have higher power:<br>the same N gives a more precise answer.</p>
<p class="key-support">Same L1 values: analysed as unrelated groups, 95% CI −33.6 to +12.8; as the paired design they came from, −23.2 to +2.3. Plan pairs or blocks when a shared source of variation exists — and analyse them as such.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 17:05–17:06 (1 minute).**

**Say:** Generalise the previous slide. Splitting each preparation into a vehicle and a Q tube — or running both conditions on the same day, plate or animal — lets the shared variation cancel in the comparison. The same twelve tubes then give a narrower interval and a higher chance of detecting a real effect, so fewer independent units are needed for the same precision. This links back to the power block in this session. Two conditions: the shared source must be real (same preparation, day, donor or litter), and the analysis must keep the pairing; a paired design analysed as unrelated groups throws the advantage away. Pairing only helps when the paired units actually resemble each other.

**Conceptual point:** Blocking removes shared, irrelevant variation from the treatment comparison, which increases precision and power for a given N.

**Likely misconception:** Pairing always helps regardless of whether the units share variation, or the analysis can choose paired or unpaired after seeing which gives the smaller p.

**Sources:** Lazic (2016) *Experimental Design for Laboratory Biologists*, ch. 3 (blocking); Festing & Altman (2002) *ILAR J* 43:244. Interval values from the counterfactual comparison on the previous slide.
:::

## Four doses: should we run six separate tests? {#four-doses}

<img class="data-plot tests-plot" src="figures/generated/tests-dose.png" alt="Raw observations and mean bars for control, low, medium and high dose." /><p class="takeaway fragment">Represent the group means together in one model.</p>
<p class="small fragment">ANOVA belongs to the linear-model framework.</p>
<p class="fine">Simulated independent cultures · 8 per group · continuous activity.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 17:06–17:08 (2 minutes).**

**Say:** Ask why four groups yield six pairs and reconnect to the multiplicity block. A group indicator linear model represents the four means together; classical one-way ANOVA tests a restriction on those means. A two-group equal-variance t-test is a special case of that classical framework. Do not quietly equate an ordinary homoscedastic linear-model fit with Welch: unequal variances can require Welch-type or other suitable inference. A common model does not by itself eliminate multiplicity.

**Conceptual point:** Several means can be represented coherently in one model.

**Likely misconception:** ANOVA is unrelated to mean-difference models, or automatically fixes all multiple testing.

**Optional follow-up:** Which of the six comparisons did the biology motivate?

**Sources:** Rebuilt using CONTENT_MAP.md concepts: experimental units and pairing (A pp. 121–144), models and assumptions (A pp. 115–160), design and sampling (R pp. 45–62), and prospective planning (D pp. 45–46, 52). Numerical examples are newly generated or explicitly reuse the original L1 data. Method checks: official R t.test, lm and wilcox.test documentation; see SESSION2_TESTS_NOTES.md.
:::

## Does Q have the same effect in both genotypes? {#genotype-interaction}

<img class="data-plot tests-plot" src="figures/generated/tests-interaction.png" alt="Mean control and Q activity by genotype; Q lowers wild-type activity more than knockout activity." /><p class="takeaway fragment">Interaction: does the Q effect depend on genotype?</p>
<p class="small fragment">Compare the effects—not their significance labels.</p>
<p class="fine">Simulated independent cultures · genotype × treatment · 8 cultures per cell.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 17:08–17:11 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Ask participants to compare slopes before naming interaction. The fitted Q effect is −27.9 in wild type and −4.8 in knockout; knockout minus wild-type effect is +23.0 activity units (model-based 95% CI approximately 11.8 to 34.2). A factorial linear model estimates this difference of differences. These are independent cultures with normal equal-SD errors in the teaching generator. Genotype need not be randomized, and a genotype mechanism claim requires comparable genetic backgrounds and design. Significant in wild type but not in knockout does not itself establish different effects; assess the interaction directly, with its interval. No factorial table drill.

**Conceptual point:** An interaction is a difference between effects on a specified scale.

**Likely misconception:** Different significance labels prove a significant difference between effects.

**Optional follow-up:** Would the same interaction question be unchanged on a log scale?

**Sources:** Rebuilt using CONTENT_MAP.md concepts: experimental units and pairing (A pp. 121–144), models and assumptions (A pp. 115–160), design and sampling (R pp. 45–62), and prospective planning (D pp. 45–46, 52). Numerical examples are newly generated or explicitly reuse the original L1 data. Method checks: official R t.test, lm and wilcox.test documentation; see SESSION2_TESTS_NOTES.md.
:::

## Simple designs need fewer replicates {#simple-design-power .key-message}

<p class="key-label">Key message</p>
<p class="key-statement">Every extra group or factor costs replicates.<br>One clear comparison is the most powerful design.</p>
<p class="key-support">Detecting an interaction of the same size as a single treatment effect needs about four times as many replicates.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 17:11–17:12 (1 minute).**

**Say:** Look back at the last few slides: two groups, paired, four doses, genotype by treatment. Each step adds groups or factors, and each step spreads the same number of replicates thinner. A paired two-condition comparison concentrates all independent replication on one question; that is why it needs the smallest N. Comparisons among several doses or genotypes need more units per group, and an interaction — a difference between two effects — is estimated with roughly twice the SE of a main effect, so detecting one of the same size needs about four times the sample size. Before adding conditions, ask whether each one serves the primary question.

**Conceptual point:** Statistical power is spent per question. Additional groups, factors and comparisons each consume independent replication.

**Likely misconception:** Adding more conditions to one experiment is free, or a factorial design automatically answers every question with the same N.

**Sources:** Gelman (2018) 'You need 16 times the sample size to estimate an interaction than to estimate a main effect' (statmodeling blog) — 4× for an interaction of equal magnitude; Lazic (2016) *Experimental Design for Laboratory Biologists*, ch. 3.
:::

## Time-course experiments: showing the effect vs. testing it {#timecourse-problem .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Discuss with a neighbour · 2 minutes</p>
<img class="data-plot tests-plot" src="figures/generated/timecourse-example.png" alt="Two overlaid time courses, Vehicle and Compound Q, with shaded ±SE bands across six time points 0 to 24 hours." />
<p class="small">Each preparation is split into tubes; one Vehicle and one Q tube are harvested at each time point.</p>
<p class="takeaway fragment">Time points from the same preparation share its biology — they are not independent comparisons.</p>
<p class="small fragment">Two-way ANOVA on time × treatment treats them as if they were.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 17:12–17:15 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Two minutes in pairs, then collect two or three answers. Most will say six tests or one two-way ANOVA. The problem with six separate tests: every time point draws its tubes from the same preparations, so the comparisons are correlated and the false positive rate is inflated unless corrected. The problem with two-way ANOVA: it assumes all measurements are independent observations. A lysate assay cannot measure one tube twice, so each time point is a separate tube — but tubes harvested at 2 h and 24 h from the same preparation share its biology, handling, passage and any uncontrolled drift. They are related, not independent. A standard two-way ANOVA ignores that correlation entirely. Time-courses are almost always pioneering experiments — you are watching when and how an effect develops. That is exploration, not confirmation.

**Conceptual point:** Time points derived from the same preparation are not independent data points; the analysis must respect that structure.

**Likely misconception:** Two-way ANOVA automatically handles repeated measures, or each time point can be tested independently without multiplicity cost.

**Optional follow-up:** At which time point would you actually want to make a claim — and did you decide that before running the experiment?

**Sources:** Rebuilt using CONTENT_MAP.md concepts: experimental units and pairing (A pp. 121–144); design and sampling (R pp. 45–62). Gelman & Hill, Ch. 11–12 (hierarchical structure); Lazic 2016 (pseudoreplication in time-series).
:::

## A time-course is most honest as exploration {#timecourse-analysis}

<div class="research-paths">
<div><p class="small"><strong>Explore</strong></p><p>Show the curve. Report no p-value.<br>You are watching biology unfold.</p></div>
<div><p class="small"><strong>Pre-specify one time point</strong></p><p>Decide before seeing the data.<br>Test that one point. If several points were planned, correct for multiple testing (e.g. Holm).</p></div>
<div><p class="small"><strong>Summarise the curve</strong></p><p>AUC or kinetic parameter per unit<br>→ one number per preparation → t-test that.</p></div>
</div>
<p class="takeaway">If testing, collapse the curve to one number per unit first.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 17:15–17:17 (2 minutes).**

**Say:** Present these as three legitimate routes, not a hierarchy. Most time-course experiments in this audience's work are genuinely exploratory — the researcher wants to know whether the effect builds, peaks, or reverses. That is valuable science; it does not require a p-value. If the biological question really is about a specific time point — for example, the moment of peak inhibition as established by prior literature — pre-specify it before collecting data and test once. If multiple time points were pre-planned, apply FWER correction such as Holm. If the shape of the whole curve matters, reduce each experimental unit to one derived number first: AUC summarises total exposure; a rate constant or half-maximum time captures kinetics. Each unit then gives one observation and you can run an ordinary t-test or regression on those derived values. Do not test every time point and report only the significant ones.

**Conceptual point:** Reducing repeated measurements to a single biologically meaningful summary per unit resolves both the independence and multiplicity problems simultaneously.

**Likely misconception:** AUC loses information compared with testing all time points; or pre-specifying one time point is arbitrary.

**Optional follow-up:** For your own time-course data, which summary would best capture the biological question?

**Sources:** Rebuilt using CONTENT_MAP.md concepts: experimental units and pairing (A pp. 121–144); design and sampling (R pp. 45–62). Matthews et al. 1990 (summarise-then-test for serial measurements); Lazic 2016 Ch. 9.
:::

## Do 100 cells from one culture give N = 100? {#hundred-cells}

<div class="tests-chain">One culture → shared conditions → 100 cell measurements</div>
<p class="takeaway">More rows do not necessarily mean more independent information.</p>
<div class="tests-grid"><p>Summarize at the experimental-unit level, when appropriate</p><p>Model clustering or repeated measurements explicitly</p></div>

::: notes
**Time: 17:17–17:19 (2 minutes).**

**Say:** Retrieve pseudoreplication. Cells from a common culture can share biology and handling; repeated measurements of an animal share that animal. Appropriate unit summaries can answer a unit-level question, but discard some information and need scientifically sensible weighting. Hierarchical or mixed-effects models can represent shared variation and repeated structure when supported by enough independent units. A mixed model cannot manufacture independent biological replication from a single culture or resolve treatment perfectly confounded with culture. Distinguish repeated times from independent repeated experiments.

**Conceptual point:** The model or aggregation must respect shared sources of variation.

**Likely misconception:** A mixed model makes any number of cultures sufficient.

**Optional follow-up:** What would another hundred cells add compared with another independent culture?

**Sources:** Rebuilt using CONTENT_MAP.md concepts: experimental units and pairing (A pp. 121–144), models and assumptions (A pp. 115–160), design and sampling (R pp. 45–62), and prospective planning (D pp. 45–46, 52). Numerical examples are newly generated or explicitly reuse the original L1 data. Method checks: official R t.test, lm and wilcox.test documentation; see SESSION2_TESTS_NOTES.md.
:::

## Does a normality test tell you which analysis to use? {#normality-gate .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Vote before the reveal</p>
<div class="tests-grid"><p>Shapiro–Wilk p &gt; 0.05<br>↓<br>t-test?</p><p>Shapiro–Wilk p &lt; 0.05<br>↓<br>Mann–Whitney?</p></div>
<p class="takeaway fragment">No: this is not a sound automatic decision rule.</p>
<p class="small">The normality assumption applies to the <strong>population</strong> — not to whether your sample looks bell-shaped.</p>
<p class="small">Small N can hide important departures.<br>Large N can detect practically unimportant departures.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 17:19–17:22 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Collect a vote before revealing the answer. Failure to reject normality does not verify it. At small N there is little information about tails; at large N a tiny deviation can be detectable without invalidating mean inference. The relevant issue is adequacy of the model and sampling distribution for the intended estimate, not ritual use of a preliminary significance test. Robustness depends on sample size, skewness, outliers, allocation balance and variance patterns. Selecting an analysis through a preliminary test can also alter the operating properties of the whole procedure. Plots diagnose structure and problems; they cannot prove normality.

**Conceptual point:** Check assumptions in relation to the intended inference rather than using a normality p-value as a switch.

**Likely misconception:** p above .05 proves a normal population.

**Optional follow-up:** Does a normality test tell you whether the observations are independent?

**Sources:** Rebuilt using CONTENT_MAP.md concepts: experimental units and pairing (A pp. 121–144), models and assumptions (A pp. 115–160), design and sampling (R pp. 45–62), and prospective planning (D pp. 45–46, 52). Numerical examples are newly generated or explicitly reuse the original L1 data. Method checks: official R t.test, lm and wilcox.test documentation; see SESSION2_TESTS_NOTES.md.
:::

## Delete it? Transform? Switch the test? {#extreme-observation .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">What evidence would you seek first?</p>
<img class="data-plot tests-plot" src="figures/generated/tests-outlier.png" alt="Eight illustrative culture measurements, one extreme activity value." /><p class="takeaway">First investigate why the observation is extreme.</p>
<p class="small">Recording error? Prespecified QC failure? Biology? Model mismatch?</p>

::: notes
**Time: 17:22–17:24 (2 minutes).**

**Say:** Ask what evidence participants would seek before changing the analysis. This is a constructed dataset, not another alteration of the original assay. Check the source record, assay calibration, sample identity and prespecified QC criteria. Correct a verified recording error with an audit trail; exclusions require a defensible reason. A genuine extreme biological observation may matter to the mean and target population. Transformation changes the scale and often the effect quantity; a rank method answers another question. Sensitivity analyses can show influence, but report data-dependent choices and all relevant results. Never delete solely because a p-value improves.

**Conceptual point:** Investigate the generating process before selecting a remedy.

**Likely misconception:** An extreme point is automatically an error or a reason to use Mann–Whitney.

**Optional follow-up:** What would you report if you could not establish why it was extreme?

**Sources:** Rebuilt using CONTENT_MAP.md concepts: experimental units and pairing (A pp. 121–144), models and assumptions (A pp. 115–160), design and sampling (R pp. 45–62), and prospective planning (D pp. 45–46, 52). Numerical examples are newly generated or explicitly reuse the original L1 data. Method checks: official R t.test, lm and wilcox.test documentation; see SESSION2_TESTS_NOTES.md.
:::

## When the effect is multiplicative, use the log scale {#log-scale-multiplicative}

<img class="data-plot" src="figures/generated/log-scale-compare.png" alt="Two-panel figure. Left: line plot showing a 3-fold up (baseline 100 to treated 300) and a 3-fold down (baseline 100 to treated 33) change on an absolute scale — the upward change appears much larger. Right: bar chart of the same changes as log₂ fold change, showing +1.58 and −1.58 symmetrically." />
<p class="takeaway">A fold change is already a ratio — the log scale treats equal folds equally.</p>
<p class="fine">Left: absolute scale. Three-fold up = +200; three-fold down = −67. Asymmetric on this scale. Right: log₂ fold change. Both are ±1.58. RNA-seq log₂ fold change applies this directly. For the L1 enzyme assay, absolute differences are appropriate — effects are small and baselines similar.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 17:24–17:27 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Ask participants to predict what three-fold up and three-fold down look like on an absolute scale before revealing the left panel. Show the asymmetry: from a baseline of 100, three-fold up is +200 while three-fold down is only −67. The visual impression on the absolute scale is that the upward effect is roughly three times the downward effect — but both represent the same fold change. On the log₂ scale, both are ±1.58, which is why RNA-seq analysis uses log₂ fold change as standard. Connect to what they already know: when a paper reports "2-fold induction," that is a ratio, and ratios should be compared on the log scale. Briefly note that for the L1 enzyme data, absolute differences are appropriate: the baseline range is narrow (79–113 U/mg), effects are small fractions of baseline, and U/mg differences are directly interpretable. The choice depends on whether effects are expected to compound multiplicatively or add linearly across the measurement range.

**Conceptual point:** Proportional effects should be analysed and displayed on a log scale; additive effects on an absolute scale. Using the wrong scale creates visual asymmetry that misrepresents the biology.

**Likely misconception:** Log transformations "just normalise" data. The choice of scale reflects a biological model about how effects work.

**Optional follow-up:** In your own assay: do you expect a 10% change at a high baseline to correspond to a 10% change at a low baseline, or the same absolute unit change regardless of baseline?

**Sources:** Smyth (2004) *Stat Appl Genet Mol Biol* 3:Article3 — motivation for log transformation in expression data; Bland & Altman (1996) *BMJ* 312:1079 — on logarithmic transformation in medical research.
:::

## What does chopping the y-axis do? {#truncated-axis .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Which panel shows the larger effect? · 1 minute</p>
<img class="data-plot" src="figures/generated/bar-truncated.png" alt="Side-by-side bar charts of Vehicle and Compound Q mean enzyme activity. Left panel: y-axis from 0 to 130 — the bars are similar heights and the difference looks modest. Right panel: y-axis from 70 to 115 — the bars appear dramatically different although the underlying data are identical." />
<p class="takeaway">Same data. A bar chart encodes length from zero — a truncated axis is a visual distortion.</p>
<p class="fine">Both panels show the same L1 enzyme experiment. A dot plot or line plot with a marked non-zero baseline can legitimately start elsewhere; a bar chart cannot.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 17:27–17:30 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Ask which panel shows the larger effect. Wait for a show of hands, then confirm: they are identical data. The right panel truncates the y-axis at 70, so the visible bar lengths represent roughly 27 and 17 units instead of 97 and 87. The visual height ratio is about 1.6; the actual ratio is about 1.1. The bar chart uses visual area as its information — cropping it at an arbitrary point changes that information without changing the numbers. For line plots and dot plots, a non-zero baseline with clearly labelled axes can be legitimate when the data range is far above zero; the bar chart is the problem because the bar's length is its encoding, and it starts at zero by convention. Ask participants to find an example in a paper they know.

**Conceptual point:** Bar chart area encodes a quantity from zero. Cropping the y-axis distorts the visual encoding while leaving the axis labels technically accurate.

**Likely misconception:** Starting the axis at a nonzero value is always acceptable if the axis is labelled. For bar charts it is not.

**Optional follow-up:** What chart type would be appropriate if the biologically relevant range for this assay is 70–115 U/mg?

**Sources:** Weissgerber et al. (2015) *PLOS Biol* 13:e1002128 "Beyond Bar and Line Graphs"; Drummond & Vowler (2011) *J Physiol* 589:1929–1931.
:::

## When values span orders of magnitude {#wide-range-log .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Which panel lets you compare all four conditions? · 1 minute</p>
<img class="data-plot" src="figures/generated/axis-break-vs-log.png" alt="Two bar charts of simulated cytokine release across four conditions. Left: linear scale — the three low-value bars are barely visible next to the stimulated bar. Right: log₁₀ scale — all four bars are legible and proportional differences are preserved." />
<p class="takeaway">An axis break removes the middle of the scale — log scale preserves it.</p>
<p class="small">Publications often use a gap symbol (⁄⁄) to skip the empty middle of the y-axis. This hides how far apart the values really are. Log scale is the honest alternative when effects are proportional.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 17:30–17:33 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Ask which panel lets them compare all four conditions meaningfully. On the linear scale, the three low-value bars are barely visible — they look identical even though low and high dose differ by four-fold. Publications often solve this by cutting out the middle of the y-axis with a break symbol. That removes the true distance between values from the visual — a reader cannot tell how far the stimulated bar is from the others. Log scale is the correct solution when data span more than one order of magnitude: on a log scale, equal vertical distances mean equal fold changes. The stimulated condition is about 80-fold above unstimulated. On the linear scale that relationship is invisible; on the log scale it is clearly encoded. Axis breaks are tempting and look authoritative in papers — point out they are almost always a sign that log scale should have been used instead.

**Conceptual point:** When values span several orders of magnitude, proportional differences are the relevant comparison — and log scale displays them honestly.

**Likely misconception:** A broken y-axis with a gap symbol is an acceptable solution. It removes scale information the reader needs.

**Optional follow-up:** For your own data: does a two-fold difference at a high baseline mean the same thing biologically as a two-fold difference at a low baseline?

**Sources:** Tufte (2001) *The Visual Display of Quantitative Information* pp. 53–77; Bland & Altman (1996) *BMJ* 312:1079 — log transformation for proportional differences.
:::

## Many lab measurements belong on a log scale {#log-measurements .key-message}

<p class="key-label">Key message</p>
<p class="key-statement">Fluorescence, RNA and protein levels, cytokines, counts:<br>analyse and plot them on a log scale.</p>
<p class="key-support">These quantities change by factors, not fixed amounts, and their spread grows with their level. On the log scale fold changes become symmetric and comparable.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 17:33–17:34 (1 minute).**

**Say:** Tie the last two slides together. Most quantities measured in a life-science lab — fluorescence intensity, qPCR and RNA-seq expression, Western blot or ELISA signals, cytokine concentrations, cell or colony counts — behave multiplicatively: treatments change them by a factor, and higher levels vary more. Log-transform before computing means, intervals and tests, and plot on a log axis. Report results as fold changes, back-transformed from the log scale. The L1 enzyme assay is an exception only because the effect is small relative to a narrow baseline range.

**Conceptual point:** The scale of analysis should match how the biology changes: proportional changes call for a log scale.

**Likely misconception:** Log transformation is a cosmetic trick to make data look normal, or is only needed for RNA-seq.

**Sources:** Bland & Altman (1996) *BMJ* 312:1079; Keene (1995) *Stat Med* 14:811 — the log transformation is special.
:::

## Three error bars. Three different claims. {#error-bars-which}

<img class="data-plot" src="figures/generated/error-bars-comparison.png" alt="Three panels each showing Vehicle and Compound Q group means. Left panel: ± SD error bars (widest). Centre panel: ± SEM error bars (narrower). Right panel: ± 95% CI error bars (widest for this small n). The widths differ substantially across panels." />
<p class="takeaway">An unlabelled error bar tells you nothing. Label it — or the reader has to guess.</p>
<p class="fine">Same six L1 preparations throughout. SD: spread of individual preparations. SEM: precision of the group mean. 95% CI: range of effect sizes compatible with the data. Each answers a different question.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 17:34–17:37 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Cover the panel titles and ask what the bars mean. Reveal them. SD is the spread in the raw data — it describes biological variability and stays roughly constant as n increases. SEM is SD/√n — it shrinks as you add replicates regardless of the biology and describes estimation precision. A 95% CI is wider than SEM (approximately ±t·SEM for small n) and describes the range of effect sizes the data cannot rule out — which is what a reader needs to assess a claim. For six preparations, the CI is notably wider than the SEM. The rule from Part 1: use SD to describe how variable the preparations are; when reporting an effect, give the SEM or, better, the 95% CI — and always say which. The problem is not SEM itself but an unlabelled bar, or SEM used to describe variability, which makes the data look less variable than they are. Recall from Part 1: report the CI or SE with the effect estimate, not the SD alone, when your reader needs to know how precisely the effect is known.

**Conceptual point:** Error bars describe fundamentally different quantities. Swapping them or leaving them unlabelled misleads the reader.

**Likely misconception:** Smaller error bars always mean a better experiment. SEM shrinks with n regardless of biological effect size.

**Optional follow-up:** In the papers you read this week, were the error bars labelled?

**Sources:** Cumming, Fidler & Vaux (2007) *J Cell Biol* 177:7–11; Vaux (2012) *Nature* 492:210–181.
:::

## What does an honest figure let you do? {#honest-figure .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">What can you do with the right panel that you cannot with the left? · 2 minutes</p>
<div style="display:flex; gap:28px; align-items:flex-start; margin-top:10px;">
<div style="flex:1; text-align:center;"><img style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" src="figures/generated/bar-conventional.png" alt="Bar chart of Vehicle and Compound Q mean enzyme activity with SEM error bars and jittered individual points. The pairing between preparations is invisible."/><p class="small" style="margin-top:8px; color:var(--muted);">Bar chart · means ± SEM · pairing invisible</p></div>
<div style="flex:1; text-align:center;"><img style="width:100%; border-radius:4px;" src="figures/generated/bio-pairs.png" alt="Paired dot plot showing enzyme activity for all six L1 preparations under Vehicle and Compound Q conditions, with connecting lines showing the direction of each preparation's response."/><p class="small" style="margin-top:8px; color:var(--muted);">Paired plot · individual preparations · direction readable</p></div>
</div>
<p class="takeaway">A good figure lets a careful reader re-examine the raw evidence.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 17:37–17:40 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Allow two minutes in pairs, then collect answers. With the right panel, a reader can: see each individual preparation; see which preparations responded consistently; check whether one preparation is driving the result; verify the direction; mentally reproduce the paired analysis. With the left panel, a reader sees only group means and one aggregate uncertainty measure. The jitter in the bar chart does not show which Vehicle and Compound Q dots came from the same preparation — the pairing is invisible. The honest figure is not more complicated: it displays the same six values each, but preserves the experimental structure. Invite a brief discussion of whether participants' most recent submitted figure would pass this test.

**Conceptual point:** A figure is honest when a careful reader can assess the underlying observations and their structure, not just the summary.

**Likely misconception:** Adding jitter to a bar chart makes it equivalent to showing individual data. It does not — it destroys the pairing information.

**Optional follow-up:** Which of the four issues we discussed applies most directly to a figure you plan to include in your next paper?

**Sources:** Weissgerber et al. (2015) *PLOS Biol* 13:e1002128; Drummond & Vowler (2011) *J Physiol* 589:2229–1931; Tukey (1977) *Exploratory Data Analysis* — the paired plot originates in Tukey's exploratory tradition.
:::

## “Compound R suppresses inflammation” {#r-lab-meeting .interaction}

<p class="small">LPS-stimulated macrophages were treated with vehicle or compound R (10 µM, 24 h).<br>IL-6 in the supernatant was measured by ELISA.</p>
<img class="data-plot workshop-plot" src="figures/generated/workshop-report.png" alt="Lab-meeting bar chart: IL-6 about 830 pg/mL with vehicle and 480 pg/mL with compound R, tiny SEM error bars, three stars." />
<p class="takeaway">*** p &lt; 0.001 &nbsp;·&nbsp; n = 3 &nbsp;·&nbsp; representative of independent experiments</p>
<p class="prompt-tag">Would you believe this conclusion?</p>

::: notes
**Time: 17:40–17:42 (2 minutes).**

**Say:** Present this as a colleague's lab-meeting slide, not a trap. Give participants a minute to react without correcting them. Most will find it convincing: a clean 40% reduction, tiny error bars, three stars, and the reassuring legend "representative of independent experiments". Do not reveal anything yet. Instructor-only provenance: the figure shows day 1 of four experiments; n = 3 are the three ELISA wells of one supernatant per condition; the Welch t-test on those wells gives p = 0.00008. The entire scenario is fictional teaching data (scripts/generate_workshop.R).

**Conceptual point:** A p-value, an n and a tidy figure do not define the evidence.

**Likely misconception:** Small error bars and many stars mean a reliable result.

**Optional follow-up:** What is your first reaction, and what would change it?

**Facilitation:** Participant reasoning takes priority over instructor explanation. Use these notes selectively; do not read them aloud. This is a fictional teaching scenario, not a published biological finding.
:::

## What do you need to know before interpreting this? {#r-information-first .interaction}

<p class="question">Ask the researcher.</p><p class="small">Collect questions before offering advice.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 17:42–17:45 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Let participants supply questions for about two minutes, then group them for one minute. Do not show a checklist. Listen for: what does n = 3 count; how many independent experiments; what does "representative" mean and how was it chosen; were vehicle and R run on the same day; were other readouts measured; were any experiments or values left out; was the analysis planned in advance. Answer that the next slides reveal the details. Reward requests for provenance; avoid treating the researcher as dishonest — every step here is common practice.

**Conceptual point:** Seek information before judging a result or prescribing an analysis.

**Likely misconception:** The only missing detail is the name of the test.

**Optional follow-up:** What in the lab notebook would answer most of these questions?

**Facilitation:** Participant reasoning takes priority over instructor explanation. Use these notes selectively; do not read them aloud. This is a fictional teaching scenario, not a published biological finding.
:::

## What was actually repeated? {#r-hierarchy .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Guess each layer before revealing</p>
<div class="workshop-hierarchy">
<p class="fragment">Four experiments, on four different days</p>
<p class="fragment">Each day: fresh macrophages, LPS, one vehicle well and one R well</p>
<p class="fragment">Each culture well → supernatant → three ELISA wells</p>
<p class="fragment">The figure shows day 1 only. n = 3 counts its ELISA wells.</p></div>
<p class="takeaway">What is the experimental unit — and how many are there?</p>

::: notes
**Time: 17:45–17:47 (2 minutes).**

**Say:** Reveal each layer after asking for a guess. Each day a fresh culture is stimulated and one well receives vehicle, one R: the culture well is the experimental unit, and the day is the independent replicate of the comparison. The three ELISA wells measure the same supernatant; they describe pipetting and plate precision, not biology. So the reported n = 3 and p < 0.001 describe how reproducible the ELISA is on day 1. The honest n for the treatment effect is the number of experiments — four, or three after the exclusion we will see next. "Representative" meant the clearest-looking day. Link back to Part 1: these are technical triplicates presented as replicates.

**Conceptual point:** Technical replicates measure the assay; independent experiments measure the biology.

**Likely misconception:** Three ELISA wells are three biological replicates, or a representative experiment stands for all of them.

**Optional follow-up:** Which metadata would have shown this immediately?

**Facilitation:** Participant reasoning takes priority over instructor explanation. Use these notes selectively; do not read them aloud. This is a fictional teaching scenario, not a published biological finding.
:::

## “Day 4 was left out — the stimulation didn't work.” {#r-exclusion .interaction}

<p class="question">What would you need to know?</p>
<p class="small fragment">Decided after the results were seen. No rule was set in advance,<br>and no unstimulated control was run to check the stimulation.</p>
<p class="small fragment">Vehicle IL-6 on day 4: 501 pg/mL — the lowest, but days 1–3 ranged from 834 to 2444.<br>On day 4, R did not lower IL-6.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 17:47–17:49 (2 minutes).**

**Say:** Ask what would make the exclusion legitimate before revealing the details. A valid exclusion needs a reason that is independent of the treatment result and, ideally, a rule written down before the data came in — for example, "an experiment counts only if LPS raises IL-6 at least ten-fold over an unstimulated well". Here there was no rule and no unstimulated well, so "the stimulation didn't work" cannot be checked. Vehicle IL-6 on day 4 was lower than on other days, but day 1 was not much higher. The decision was made after seeing that R had no effect that day. Do not accuse the researcher of misconduct: this is a very common, well-intended judgement. The next slides show how much it matters.

**Conceptual point:** Exclusions need a reason independent of the outcome, ideally a rule fixed in advance.

**Likely misconception:** Any experiment that "looks wrong" may be dropped, or no experiment may ever be excluded.

**Optional follow-up:** Which control would have made the day-4 decision checkable?

**Facilitation:** Participant reasoning takes priority over instructor explanation. Use these notes selectively; do not read them aloud. This is a fictional teaching scenario, not a published biological finding.
:::

## Look at all four experiments {#r-all-days .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Which panel shows what R did? · 2 minutes</p>
<img class="data-plot workshop-plot" src="figures/generated/workshop-all-days.png" alt="Left: IL-6 pooled over four days as bars with large SEM error bars; vehicle and R overlap. Right: the same data on a log scale, paired by day; R is lower than vehicle on days 1 to 3, slightly higher on day 4, which is dashed and marked as dropped." />
<p class="takeaway fragment">IL-6 varies five-fold between days — but within days 1–3, R was always lower.</p>
<p class="fine">Each point = one culture well (mean of its three ELISA wells). Dashed: day 4, dropped by the researcher.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 17:49–17:52 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Give pairs two minutes. On the left, the days are pooled on a linear scale with SEM: the day-to-day differences in IL-6 (about 500 to 2400 pg/mL) swamp the treatment effect and the bars overlap. On the right, the same eight values are paired by day and plotted on a log scale: within each of days 1–3, R lowered IL-6 by roughly 25–40%, while on day 4 it did not. Connect three key messages: pair or block by day, use a log scale for cytokines, and show the individual experiments. Ask what a reader would conclude from each panel.

**Conceptual point:** Pairing by day removes day-to-day variation; the log scale shows proportional changes; individual experiments make the exclusion visible.

**Likely misconception:** Pooled bars with SEM are an honest summary of an experiment run on several days.

**Optional follow-up:** Which panel would you put in the paper — and what would you write about day 4?

**Facilitation:** Participant reasoning takes priority over instructor explanation. Use these notes selectively; do not read them aloud. This is a fictional teaching scenario, not a published biological finding.
:::

## Analyse the experiment, not the ELISA wells {#r-reanalysis}

<img class="data-plot workshop-plot" src="figures/generated/workshop-fold-changes.png" alt="IL-6 fold change R over vehicle, one point per experiment day. Days 1 to 3: mean fold 0.65, 95 percent CI 0.46 to 0.92, p 0.03. All four days: mean fold 0.74, 95 percent CI 0.46 to 1.18, p 0.14." />
<p class="takeaway">Reported: p &lt; 0.001. Per experiment: p = 0.03 — or p = 0.14 if day 4 stays in.</p>
<p class="small">One fold change per experiment, paired by day, on the log scale. The decision about day 4 matters more than the choice of test.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 17:52–17:55 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Walk through the three numbers. The reported p < 0.001 came from ELISA wells of one day. The appropriate analysis uses one value per experiment: the log fold change R/vehicle within each day, then a paired (one-sample) t-test on those values. With days 1–3: IL-6 fell to 0.65 of vehicle (95% CI 0.46 to 0.92), p = 0.03. With all four days: 0.74 (0.46 to 1.18), p = 0.14. The estimate barely moves; the interval and the p-value do. Point out that the after-the-fact exclusion is exactly what moves p across 0.05. Neither version supports a confident claim: three or four experiments give a wide interval. The data are compatible with anything from a 50% reduction to no effect.

**Conceptual point:** The analysis must use the independent experiments as units; with few experiments, post-hoc decisions can decide the conclusion.

**Likely misconception:** A more appropriate test would have rescued the result.

**Optional follow-up:** Which of the two versions would you report, and how would you mention the other?

**Facilitation:** Participant reasoning takes priority over instructor explanation. Use these notes selectively; do not read them aloud. This is a fictional teaching scenario, not a published biological finding.
:::

## IL-6, TNF and IL-1β were measured. Why report only IL-6? {#r-cytokines .interaction}

<img class="data-plot workshop-plot" src="figures/generated/workshop-cytokines.png" alt="Fold change R over vehicle per experiment day for three cytokines. IL-6 lower on days 1 to 3; TNF and IL-1 beta scattered around 1." />
<p class="takeaway fragment">Choosing the readout after seeing the data makes IL-6 an exploratory finding.</p>
<p class="fine">One point per experiment day. Open circles: day 4.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 17:55–17:57 (2 minutes).**

**Say:** Reveal that the ELISA panel also measured TNF and IL-1β, which showed no consistent change. IL-6 was reported because it "worked". That is not dishonest by intention, but it turns the experiment into a search: with three readouts the chance that at least one looks convincing by chance is higher than for one pre-chosen readout. The IL-6 signal is a reasonable hypothesis for a new experiment, with IL-6 named as the primary readout in advance. Also note the biology: an anti-inflammatory compound that lowers IL-6 but not TNF or IL-1β calls for a narrower claim than "suppresses inflammation".

**Conceptual point:** Selecting one readout from several after seeing the data turns confirmation into exploration.

**Likely misconception:** Unreported readouts are irrelevant to the one that is reported.

**Optional follow-up:** How would you report all three cytokines honestly?
