**Facilitation:** Participant reasoning takes priority over instructor explanation. Use these notes selectively; do not read them aloud. This is a fictional teaching scenario, not a published biological finding.
:::

## “Suppresses inflammation” — what can these data support? {#r-claim .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Choose the strongest claim you could defend to a reviewer</p>
<div class="workshop-claims"><p>R suppresses inflammation</p><p>R lowers IL-6, TNF and IL-1β</p><p>R lowered IL-6 in LPS-stimulated macrophages in 3 of 4 experiments — worth a planned repeat</p><p>R is anti-inflammatory in patients</p></div>

::: notes
**Time: 17:57–17:59 (2 minutes).**

**Say:** Ask for votes and one reason each. Only the third option matches the evidence: one cell type, one stimulus, one dose, one readout, a consistent reduction in three of four experiments and an interval that still includes no effect. "Suppresses inflammation" generalises from one cytokine to a biological process; TNF and IL-1β contradict it. Patients are far outside the experimental space. Link back to the Part 1 population question: the claim follows what was sampled and measured, not the p-value.

**Conceptual point:** The scope of a claim follows the design, the readouts and the uncertainty — not statistical significance.

**Likely misconception:** A significant p-value licenses the broad mechanistic claim in the title.

**Optional follow-up:** What would need to be added before "anti-inflammatory" is justified?

**Facilitation:** Participant reasoning takes priority over instructor explanation. Use these notes selectively; do not read them aloud. This is a fictional teaching scenario, not a published biological finding.
:::

## Done correctly, the answer is usually less exciting {#less-exciting .key-message}

<p class="key-label">Key message</p>
<p class="key-statement">Done correctly, the answer is usually<br>less exciting than the first impression.</p>
<p class="key-support">“R suppresses inflammation, p &lt; 0.001” became “R lowered IL-6 in 3 of 4 experiments — worth a planned repeat.” That is not a failure: it is the result that will still hold next year.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 17:59–18:00 (1 minute).**

**Say:** Name what just happened. Every correction — counting experiments instead of ELISA wells, keeping day 4, reporting all three cytokines, narrowing the claim — made the result less spectacular. This is the normal experience of doing it properly, not bad luck. Reassure the audience: a modest, honest result is publishable, a solid basis for the next experiment, and far less likely to collapse when someone else repeats it. The exciting version is the one that tends not to replicate.

**Conceptual point:** Correct analysis removes the illusory precision and selection that make results look strong; the remaining, smaller result is the reliable one.

**Likely misconception:** A less exciting result after reanalysis means the analysis was too conservative or the experiment failed.

**Sources:** Ioannidis (2005) *PLoS Med* 2:e124 — why most published research findings are false; Button et al. (2013) *Nat Rev Neurosci* 14:365 — small studies overestimate effects.
:::

## Repeat the study so it can answer the question {#r-redesign .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Pairs or small groups · 6 minutes · keywords or a sketch are enough</p>
<div class="workshop-canvas">
<p><strong>Question and primary readout</strong><br>What exactly do we want to learn? What is measured first?</p>
<p><strong>Experimental unit and N</strong><br>What is independently repeated, and how often?</p>
<p><strong>Pairing and allocation</strong><br>What should share a day or plate? How are wells assigned?</p>
<p><strong>QC and exclusions</strong><br>Which rules are fixed before the results are seen?</p>
<p><strong>Analysis and report</strong><br>Which effect, scale and interval? Which figure?</p>
</div>

::: notes
**Time: 18:00–18:06 (6 minutes).**

**Say:** Distribute workshop-design-canvas.html as a handout or keep this slide visible. Give six minutes with a one-minute warning. Circulate and ask: what is the experimental unit; how many independent experiments and why; do vehicle and R share a day and plate; what makes an experiment valid, decided in advance; what is the primary readout; which scale and figure. Accept different defensible designs. Do not supply a number for N without a relevant effect and an estimate of variability — but point out that the day-to-day variability seen here is useful planning information.

**Conceptual point:** Question, design, QC and analysis are decided together and in advance.

**Likely misconception:** There is one correct redesign, or N can be chosen without a relevant effect size.

**Optional follow-up:** What would you change if the aim were to compare several doses?

**Facilitation:** Participant reasoning takes priority over instructor explanation. Use these notes selectively; do not read them aloud. This is a fictional teaching scenario, not a published biological finding.
:::

## One defensible repeat — not the only one {#r-one-redesign}

<div class="workshop-canvas">
<p><strong>Question</strong><br>Does 10 µM R lower IL-6 in LPS-stimulated macrophages?<br>IL-6 primary; TNF and IL-1β exploratory</p>
<p><strong>Unit and N</strong><br>One culture well per condition per independent experiment<br>About 7 experiments for a 30% reduction, from the variability seen here</p>
<p><strong>Pairing</strong><br>Vehicle and R on the same day and plate; positions randomized</p>
<p><strong>QC, fixed in advance</strong><br>Include an unstimulated well; keep an experiment only if LPS raises IL-6 ≥ 10-fold</p>
<p><strong>Analysis and report</strong><br>Log fold change per experiment, paired; mean fold change with 95% CI; show every experiment</p>
</div>

::: notes
**Time: 18:06–18:09 (3 minutes).**

**Say:** Ask one group to present its design first, then compare with this example. The repeat confirms the hypothesis generated by the original data; choosing IL-6 now does not make the old result confirmatory. N: with a standard deviation of about 0.4 in log2 fold change between experiments (as in the four days here) and a relevant effect of a 30% reduction, about seven paired experiments give 80% power at α = 0.05 — this is an illustration of the planning logic, not a recommendation. The QC rule makes exclusions independent of the treatment result. ELISA triplicates are kept and averaged per culture well: they improve the measurement, not N. Add a viability readout if the claim is that R lowers IL-6 production rather than killing cells.

**Conceptual point:** A defensible repeat follows from the question; its decisions are written down before data collection.

**Likely misconception:** Selecting the primary readout now validates the earlier result.

**Optional follow-up:** Which control would you add to rule out that R simply kills the cells?

**Facilitation:** Participant reasoning takes priority over instructor explanation. Use these notes selectively; do not read them aloud. This is a fictional teaching scenario, not a published biological finding.
:::

## What improved before any test was run? {#r-what-changed .interaction}

<p class="prompt-tag">Name your most consequential change · 1 minute</p>
<div class="research-paths"><div><h3>Original report</h3><p>One “representative” day shown<br>n counted ELISA wells<br>Day 4 dropped after seeing it<br>IL-6 picked from three readouts<br>Pooled bars, linear scale</p></div><div><h3>Planned repeat</h3><p>Every experiment shown<br>n = independent experiments<br>QC rule fixed in advance<br>One primary readout<br>Paired log fold changes with CI</p></div></div>
<p class="takeaway">Most of the improvement happened before the statistical test.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 18:09–18:11 (2 minutes).**

**Say:** Ask groups for their single most consequential change and one remaining limitation. Some problems can be fixed by reanalysis now: show all four days, analyse per experiment, report both versions of the day-4 decision, report all three cytokines. Others need new data: more independent experiments, an unstimulated control, a fixed QC rule and a pre-chosen primary readout. A new experiment adds information; it is not a search for a better p-value.

**Conceptual point:** Better inference starts with design and transparent reporting, not with a different test.

**Likely misconception:** Changing the test is the main improvement.

**Optional follow-up:** Which improvement requires new data rather than a reanalysis?

**Facilitation:** Participant reasoning takes priority over instructor explanation. Use these notes selectively; do not read them aloud. This is a fictional teaching scenario, not a published biological finding.
:::

## Plan the experiment before you pipette {#plan-before-pipetting .key-message}

<p class="key-label">Key message</p>
<p class="key-statement">Good experiments are designed before the first pipetting step — not rescued afterwards.</p>
<p class="key-support">Question · experimental unit · N · pairing and blocking · QC rules · analysis: write them down first.</p>
<p class="fine">Further reading: S.E. Lazic (2016) <em>Experimental Design for Laboratory Biologists: Maximising Information and Improving Reproducibility.</em> Cambridge University Press. · D.J. Glass (2014) <em>Experimental Design for Biologists</em>, 2nd ed. Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Press.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 18:11–18:12 (1 minute).**

**Say:** Connect the comparison on the previous slide to a habit: every improvement in the planned repeat was a decision made before data collection. Recommend writing a one-page plan — question, primary readout, experimental unit, number of independent experiments, pairing or blocking, QC and exclusion rules, planned analysis — and discussing it with a colleague or statistician before starting. Point to the two books: Lazic is written for laboratory biologists and covers experimental units, pseudoreplication, blocking and power with lab examples; Glass covers the logic of hypotheses, controls and experimental strategy. Both are readable without a statistics background.

**Conceptual point:** Design decisions determine what an experiment can show; analysis can only extract what the design put in.

**Likely misconception:** Statistics is something done to the data once the experiment is finished.

**Sources:** Lazic SE (2016) *Experimental Design for Laboratory Biologists*. Cambridge University Press. Glass DJ (2014) *Experimental Design for Biologists*, 2nd ed. Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Press. Fisher RA (1938): "To consult the statistician after an experiment is finished is often merely to ask him to conduct a post mortem examination."
:::

## “My p-value is below 0.001. Is my result real?” {#r-real .interaction}

<p class="question">How would you respond now?</p>
<p class="small fragment">Tell me how the experiment was done, what was independently repeated,<br>what effect you wanted to estimate — and how this result was selected.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 18:12–18:14 (2 minutes).**

**Say:** Give participants about a minute to formulate a response, then reveal the prompt. Aim for a useful conversation rather than yes or no. The IL-6 reduction may well be real — three of four experiments point the same way — but the reported p-value describes ELISA precision on one day, and the honest evidence is weaker and depends on a post-hoc exclusion. The constructive answer is a planned repeat, not a verdict on the researcher.

**Conceptual point:** A p-value opens a conversation about design, uncertainty and selection.

**Likely misconception:** Scepticism means dismissing the data or the researcher.

**Optional follow-up:** What practical next step would you recommend first?

**Facilitation:** Participant reasoning takes priority over instructor explanation. Use these notes selectively; do not read them aloud. This is a fictional teaching scenario, not a published biological finding.
:::

## Ten things to take home {#key-messages-recap .key-message}

<p class="key-label">Key messages</p>
<ol class="key-recap">
<li>Report an effect with its SEM or, better, its 95% CI — not the SD.</li>
<li>A small p-value is not a large effect. Judge biological relevance from the effect and its interval.</li>
<li>p &gt; 0.05 does not mean no effect. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.</li>
<li>Exploration generates hypotheses; its p-values mean little. Confirm in a new experiment.</li>
<li>Record metadata — preparation, day, tube, well — for every value.</li>
<li>Paired and blocked designs have higher power. Keep the pairing in the analysis.</li>
<li>Simple designs need fewer replicates. Every extra group or factor costs power.</li>
<li>Fluorescence, RNA, protein and cytokine levels, counts: analyse on a log scale.</li>
<li>Done correctly, the answer is usually less exciting — and more likely to hold.</li>
<li>Plan the experiment before you pipette (Lazic 2016; Glass 2014).</li>
</ol>

::: notes
**Time: 18:14–18:15 (1 minute).**

**Say:** Read the ten messages without elaborating; each one was already discussed. Ask participants which one would most change how they plan or report their next experiment. Then move to the final slide.

**Conceptual point:** A compact summary of the practical rules that recur across both sessions.

**Likely misconception:** These are rigid rules. Each is a default that holds for typical laboratory experiments; the reasons were discussed where each first appeared.

**Sources:** Synthesis of key-message slides in Sessions 1 and 2.
:::

## Statistics cannot rescue an experiment that could not answer the question. {#course-landing}

<p class="question">Design the experiment and the analysis together.</p>

::: notes
**Time: 18:15–18:16 (1 minute).**

**Say:** Connect explicitly to the opening motivation: researchers often seek statistical help only after collecting data. This is an invitation to bring the biological question and protocol earlier, not a criticism of colleagues or a claim that imperfect data are worthless. Thoughtful reanalysis may recover supported comparisons; it cannot create missing independent units, identify completely confounded effects or supply absent population coverage. Ask each participant to choose one design conversation to have before the next collection. Thank them and stop here.

**Conceptual point:** Plan the evidence and its interpretation together.

**Likely misconception:** A flawed report means no useful learning or follow-up is possible.

**Optional follow-up:** What will you discuss with a collaborator before the next experiment?

**Facilitation:** Participant reasoning takes priority over instructor explanation. Use these notes selectively; do not read them aloud. This is a fictional teaching scenario, not a published biological finding.
:::
